beforeReading: Ask learners: "How deep do you think sunlight can travel into the ocean? What happens to plants when there is no light?"
Locate Tema and the Gulf of Guinea on a map and trace how the Gulf opens into the wider Atlantic Ocean.
whileReading: Pause after page 5 to calculate why a submarine needs special materials at 1,000 m depth.
Pause after page 11 to compare the energy source of a surface food chain (Sun → phytoplankton) with a vent food chain (hydrogen sulfide → chemosynthetic microbes).
afterReading: Have learners sketch a vertical chart of the ocean zones showing where sunlight ends and how organisms adapt in each layer.
discussion: Why is bioluminescence called "cold light", and how is it different from a glowing hot metal wire?
Why did scientists before 1977 assume that almost no complex life could thrive on the deep ocean floor without food falling from the sunlit surface?
Why should humanity be careful about disturbing or mining deep-sea hydrothermal vents before scientists finish studying the species that live there?
reflection: If you could design a sensor or camera for a Ghanaian research ROV exploring the deep Gulf of Guinea, what question would you want it to answer?

mathsExtension.task: Water pressure increases by about 1 atmosphere for every 10 metres of depth, plus 1 atmosphere of air pressure at the surface. What is the total pressure in atmospheres at 200 metres depth?
If a deep-sea ROV dives at a steady speed of 30 metres per minute, how many minutes will it take to reach 3,000 metres?

support: Use a clear bottle of water and a torch covered with blue cloth layers to model how light dims as depth increases.
stretch: Write a short comparison table contrasting photosynthesis and chemosynthesis across four columns: Energy source, Producers, Habitat, and Consumers.

culturalNotes: Tetteh (Ga-Dangme) and Ama / Akua / Mensah (Akan) reflect coastal and southern Ghanaian names; Tema is Ghana’s major port and marine industrial city.
localiseThis: Connect to local fish species familiar in Ghanaian markets (such as herrings/sardinella, mackerel, and tuna) that live in the sunlit zone of the Gulf of Guinea.

whatWeKnow: Sunlight sufficient for photosynthesis penetrates only the upper ~200 metres (the photic/epipelagic zone) of the ocean.
Roughly 75% of pelagic animals between 200 m and 4,000 m produce bioluminescence via luciferin-luciferase chemical reactions or symbiotic bacteria.
Hydrothermal vents (discovered in 1977) support thriving ecosystems powered by chemosynthetic microbes oxidizing hydrogen sulfide rather than using sunlight.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Over 70% of the global ocean floor remains unmapped at high acoustic resolution, and marine biologists discover hundreds of new deep-sea species every year.
Biochemists are still investigating unique enzymes and compounds in deep-sea sponges, microbes, and vent organisms that may lead to new medicines.
Ecologists are still studying how deep-sea currents, carbon storage, and potential seabed mining affect fragile abyssal habitats.

investigation.title: See How Water Depth Increases Pressure
materials: An empty 1.5-litre clear plastic water bottle
A compass point or nail (handled by the teacher)
A bucket or outdoor sink and water
steps: Have the teacher carefully poke three small, equal-sized pinholes in a vertical line down the side of the plastic bottle: one near the top (5 cm down), one in the middle (12 cm down), and one near the bottom (20 cm down).
Cover all three holes with a strip of tape and fill the bottle completely with water (leave the cap off).
Place the bottle at the edge of a table over a bucket or outdoors, peel off the tape all at once, and observe how far each stream of water shoots out horizontally.
investigation.whatToNotice: The stream from the bottom hole shoots out the farthest and fastest because there is a taller column of water pressing down above it, demonstrating how hydrostatic pressure increases with depth!
investigation.safetyNote: Only the teacher should use a sharp point to make the pinholes in the plastic bottle; perform the water test outdoors or over a bucket so floors do not become slippery.

factCheck.claim: About three-quarters of deep pelagic marine organisms produce bioluminescence using luciferin and luciferase.
factCheck.explanation: QuantitativeROV surveys from the surface to 4,000 m show ~76% of macroscopic water-column individuals have bioluminescent capability.
factCheck.reference: Martini, S., & Haddock, S. H. D. (2017). Quantification of bioluminescence from the surface to the deep sea demonstrates its predominance as an ecological trait. Scientific Reports, 7, 45750; NOAA Ocean Exploration, Bioluminescence and Deep-Sea Vents.

factCheck.claim: Hydrothermal vents host ecosystems powered by chemosynthesis rather than photosynthesis, first discovered in 1977.
factCheck.explanation: Discovered along the Galápagos Rift in 1977 and subsequently along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, vent ecosystems rely on chemoautotrophic bacteria and archaea oxidizing reduced sulfur compounds (H2S).
factCheck.reference: Corliss, J. B. et al. (1979). Submarine thermal springs on the Galápagos Rift. Science, 203(4385), 1073–1083; Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) Hydrothermal Vents Fact Sheet.

reviewerNotes: Confirm tone and double t length.
Confirm vowel quality and whether the final syllable is stressed.

teacherGuide.overview: Set near Mole National Park in northern Ghana’s Savannah Region, this Lower Primary story introduces elephant social structure (matriarchal herds), physical adaptations (ears and mud for thermoregulation), infrasound seismic communication, wildlife safety rules, and peaceful human-elephant coexistence using beehive fences.
learningGoals: Describe how African elephant families are led by a matriarch who remembers water and food routes.
Explain how elephants cool themselves using their ears and mud, and how they communicate over long distances using low rumbles (infrasound) and ground vibrations.
State clear wildlife safety rules (never approach wild elephants alone; stay quiet, downwind, and at a safe distance with a ranger).
Explain how beehive fences protect farm crops peacefully while supporting biodiversity.

beforeReading: Show Mole National Park in the Savannah Region on a map of Ghana.
Ask learners: "How do you talk to a friend who is far across the school field? How do you think elephants talk across the savannah?"
whileReading: Pause after page 3 to review the three wildlife safety rules Ranger Braimah shares.
Pause after page 7 to let learners tap their desks gently like Ranger Braimah did.
afterReading: Act out how a beehive fence works: one group plays maize plants, two learners hold an imaginary string with "beehives", and another group plays the elephant family turning safely toward the park corridor.
discussion: Why is an older grandmother elephant so important to the survival of her herd during a dry season?
Why do elephants avoid buzzing honeybees even though an elephant is huge and a bee is tiny?
reflection: What can we learn from elephant families about listening to elders and looking after younger children?

mathsExtension.task: Esi counted 6 elephants in the first family at the waterhole, and 3 more elephants walked over from the baobab trees. How many elephants were there altogether?
Mama hung 4 beehives on the north side of the maize field and 4 beehives on the east side. How many beehives did she hang in all?

support: Use pictures to match three elephant body parts (ears, trunk, foot pads) to their jobs (cooling, drinking/spraying, feeling ground rumbles).
stretch: Draw a map of a village near Mole National Park showing farms protected by beehive fences and a clear green corridor leading to the river.

culturalNotes: Mole National Park is Ghana’s largest wildlife refuge, located in the Savannah Region near Larabanga and Damongo.
Esi (Akan) and Braimah (common northern Ghanaian name) reflect everyday Ghanaian diversity.
localiseThis: Discuss any wildlife reserves, sanctuaries (such as Kakum, Mole, Boabeng-Fiema, or Wechiau), or farm protection methods known in your area.

whatWeKnow: African elephants live in matriarchal family units where the oldest female retains decades of spatial memory for water and food routes.
Elephants produce low-frequency infrasound (<20 Hz) that travels several kilometres through the air and couples into the ground as seismic waves detected via mechanoreceptors in their feet.
Beehive fences and chilli-pepper deterrents significantly reduce crop raiding without harming elephants.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Bioacousticians are still decoding the specific meanings of hundreds of different elephant rumbles, postures, and gestures across African populations.
Conservation scientists in West Africa are using satellite collars and genetic studies to map how fragmented forest and savannah elephant corridors can best be reconnected.

investigation.title: Listen to Vibrations Through Solid Wood vs Air
materials: A long wooden classroom desk or table
Your fingertips or a wooden pencil with an eraser end
steps: Have one learner sit at one end of a long wooden desk and tap the wood very softly with a fingertip so their partner standing at the other end can barely hear it through the air.
Now have the partner rest one ear gently flat against the wooden desktop (or press their palm flat on the wood) while the first learner taps with the exact same gentle force.
Compare how clear the tap sounds and feels through the solid wood compared to through the air.
investigation.whatToNotice: Vibrations travel strongly through solid materials like wood and soil, similar to how elephants sense low seismic rumbles through the ground with their feet!
investigation.safetyNote: Tap only very gently with a fingertip or eraser, never bang hard while a classmate’s ear is resting on the desk.

factCheck.claim: Elephants communicate using low-frequency infrasound rumbles and detect seismic ground vibrations through their feet.
factCheck.explanation: Elephant vocalizations include fundamental frequencies of 14–35 Hz that propagate through air and ground; elephant foot pads contain Pacinian corpuscles and acoustic fat pads sensitive to seismic vibrations.
factCheck.reference: O’Connell-Rodwell, C. E. (2007). Keeping an "Ear" to the Ground: Seismic Communication in Elephants. Physiology, 22(4), 287–294; Cornell Lab of Ornithology, Elephant Listening Project.

factCheck.claim: Beehive fences deter elephants from crop fields because elephants fear honeybee stings around their eyes and inside their trunks.
factCheck.explanation: Field trials across Africa demonstrate that elephants actively avoid African honeybees (Apis mellifera scutellata) and emit specific alarm rumbles when hearing bee buzzes.
factCheck.reference: King, L. E., Douglas-Hamilton, I., & Vollrath, F. (2007). African elephants run from the sound of disturbed bees. Current Biology, 17(19), R832–R833; Save the Elephants, Elephants and Bees Project.

Adwoa: his fourteen-year-old classmate, hair styled in neat twists with a headband, wearing the same sky-blue collared school shirt, sharp and inquisitive.
Dr Afia Boateng: a Ghanaian astrophysicist at the planetarium in Accra, wearing a deep indigo blazer over a gold-patterned top.

teacherGuide.overview: Set at the Ghana Planetarium in Accra, this JHS 2–3 story demystifies black holes using clear physics: debunking the "cosmic vacuum cleaner" myth, explaining escape velocity and the event horizon, presenting four independent lines of observational evidence (stellar orbits around Sagittarius A*, X-ray accretion disks, gravitational waves, and Event Horizon Telescope radio imaging), and highlighting open questions in quantum gravity.
learningGoals: Explain why a black hole is not a cosmic vacuum cleaner and how its gravity at a large distance matches any star of equal mass.
Define escape velocity and explain why light cannot escape from inside the event horizon.
Describe four real astronomical methods used to detect black holes (stellar orbits, accretion-disk X-rays, gravitational waves, and EHT shadow imaging).
Distinguish established relativistic physics from unresolved questions about quantum gravity and the interior of black holes.

subjectLinks.subject: Science (JHS)
subjectLinks.link: Forces, gravity, light, the solar system, stars and galaxies.

subjectLinks.subject: Mathematics (JHS)
subjectLinks.link: Speed, distance, time, large numbers, and inverse-square relationships.

subjectLinks.subject: English Language (JHS)
subjectLinks.link: Complex informational and narrative reading comprehension, scientific argumentation.

beforeReading: Ask learners: "If you throw a stone straight up, why does it come back down? How fast would you have to launch a rocket so it never falls back to Earth?"
Ask what learners have seen about black holes in movies or cartoons, and list their ideas on the board to test against evidence in the story.
whileReading: Pause after page 3 to check understanding of the Sun-replacement thought experiment.
Pause after page 11 to review the four independent lines of evidence that prove black holes exist even though the interior is dark.
afterReading: Revisit the movie myths on the board and have learners correct each one using scientific evidence from the story.
discussion: Why does Earth not get pulled into the Sun right now, and how does that same principle apply to stars orbiting a black hole at a safe distance?
Where does the stretched-cloth model of spacetime work well, and what are its limitations? (See Analogy Note in the Fact-Check Sheet.)
Why did the Event Horizon Telescope need radio dishes spread across multiple continents to photograph M87* and Sagittarius A*?
reflection: How does learning how scientists detect invisible objects in space change the way you think about solving hard problems using indirect clues?

mathsExtension.task: Earth’s escape velocity is about 11 km/s, while the speed of light is about 300,000 km/s. Approximately how many times faster than Earth’s escape velocity is the speed of light? (Round to the nearest thousand.)
Sagittarius A* is about 26,000 light-years away from Earth. How many years does it take for light or radio waves from the centre of the Milky Way to reach our telescopes?
mathsExtension.answer: 26,000 years (because 1 light-year is the distance light travels in 1 year).

support: Use the stretched-cloth and marble demonstration in class so learners can physically see stable orbits far from the central weight versus capture close to the steep centre.
stretch: Research and write a short paragraph on how Ghana’s 32-metre Kuntunse Radio Telescope contributes to Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) networks in Africa.

culturalNotes: The Ghana Planetarium in Accra has inspired thousands of Ghanaian schoolchildren in astronomy and space science.
Kofi, Adwoa, and Afia Boateng are Akan names.
localiseThis: Connect to the Ghana Planetarium (Accra) and the Ghana Radio Astronomy Observatory (Kuntunse).

whatWeKnow: Stellar-mass black holes form from the gravitational collapse of massive stars, and supermassive black holes (millions to billions of solar masses) reside at the centres of most large galaxies, including Sagittarius A* in the Milky Way.
Outside the event horizon, a black hole’s gravitational field obeys Einstein’s general relativity (and approximates Newton’s law of gravitation at large distances).
Astronomers have verified black holes through stellar orbits (2020 Nobel Prize in Physics), gravitational waves (LIGO/Virgo, 2015), X-ray accretion disks, and EHT horizon-scale images (2019, 2022).
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Physicists do not yet have a complete, experimentally verified theory of quantum gravity to describe what replaces the classical "singularity" inside a black hole.
The black hole information paradox, how quantum information is preserved when a black hole slowly evaporates via Hawking radiation, remains an active theoretical question.
Astronomers are still investigating using the James Webb Space Telescope how the earliest supermassive black holes grew so rapidly in the young universe.

investigation.title: Model Gravity and Orbits on a Stretched Cloth
materials: A large plastic basin or bucket (or four students holding the corners of a stretchy cloth taut)
A piece of stretchy T-shirt fabric or lycra cloth
A heavy smooth stone or metal ball
Two or three small glass marbles
steps: Stretch the cloth smoothly and tightly across the top of the basin (or have four learners hold the edges tight and level).
Roll a small marble straight across the flat cloth and observe that it travels in a straight line.
Place the heavy stone in the middle so the cloth curves downward into a funnel, then roll the small marble sideways near the outer edge at a moderate speed so it curves in an orbit around the stone.
Now roll the marble very slowly or aim it closely at the steep central dip and observe how it spirals inward.
investigation.whatToNotice: At a safe distance with enough sideways speed, the marble orbits around the heavy mass without getting "sucked in"; only paths that pass too close or too slowly fall into the steep central well.
investigation.safetyNote: Hold the heavy stone carefully so it does not drop onto toes, and keep small marbles off the floor so nobody slips.

factCheck.claim: Replacing the Sun with a black hole of equal mass would not suck in the Earth; Earth would maintain its orbit.
factCheck.explanation: By Birkhoff’s theorem in general relativity (and Newton’s shell theorem), the external gravitational field at distances much greater than the Schwarzschild radius (r_s ≈ 3 km for 1 solar mass) is identical to that of the Sun.
factCheck.reference: NASA Black Hole Safety & Myths FAQ; Thorne, K. S. (1994), Black Holes and Time Warps.
factCheck.analogyNote: The stretched-cloth analogy helps visualise how mass curves spacetime, but teachers should clarify that real spacetime is 4-dimensional (not a 2D sheet) and balls on a cloth slow down due to friction, whereas space is nearly frictionless.

factCheck.claim: Sagittarius A* (~4 million solar masses) and M87* have been confirmed through stellar orbits, gravitational waves, and Event Horizon Telescope radio interferometry.
factCheck.explanation: Ghez et al. and Genzel et al. tracked star S2 orbiting Sgr A* (2020 Nobel Prize); LIGO detected binary black hole mergers in 2015 (GW150914); the EHT Collaboration published direct shadow images of M87* (2019) and Sgr A* (2022).
factCheck.reference: Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration (2019, 2022), Astrophysical Journal Letters; Nobel Prize in Physics 2017 & 2020 Scientific Background.

teacherGuide.overview: Designed for Primary 1–2 learners, this schoolyard story introduces practical observation and measurement (comparing temperatures in sun vs shade), explains in child-friendly terms how trees cool their surroundings through shade and transpiration/evaporation, and models environmental teamwork through tree planting and care.
learningGoals: Observe and compare temperatures in direct sunlight versus under tree shade.
Explain two ways trees help cool a compound: blocking direct solar rays (shade) and releasing moisture from leaves that evaporates (transpiration).
Identify what young saplings need to survive (water, soil, sunlight, mulch to hold moisture, and protection from browsing animals).
Work cooperatively with classmates to care for the school environment.

Pause after page 6 and have learners blow gently on a damp hand to feel how evaporating water cools skin.

discussion: What happens to bare soil when the hot sun shines on it all day with no trees or grass?
Why did the children water the saplings early in the morning and put dry leaves (mulch) around the soil?
Why do young trees in Ghana often need a small fence or basket guard around them?
reflection: What is one thing you and your friends can do this week to care for plants or trees at school or at home?

mathsExtension.task: The temperature in the sun was 36 degrees and the temperature in the shade was 30 degrees. How many degrees cooler was the shade?
Team Green planted 4 saplings. If each sapling needs 2 cans of water in the morning, how many cans of water do they carry altogether?

support: Do the damp-hand cooling test in class: wet the back of one hand with a drop of clean water, keep the other hand dry, wave both gently, and feel which hand feels cooler.
stretch: Draw a labelled picture of a tree showing the roots drinking water, the trunk carrying it up, and the leaves making shade and cool air.

culturalNotes: Neem (Azadirachta indica) and mango trees are among the most common schoolyard and compound shade trees across Ghana; ampe is a beloved Ghanaian jumping and clapping game.
Kwame, Abena, and Akua are Akan day names.
localiseThis: Name the specific shade trees growing in your own school compound (such as neem, mango, acacia, rain tree, or almond tree).

whatWeKnow: Tree canopies intercept incoming solar radiation, reducing surface temperatures beneath them by several degrees Celsius compared to bare sunlit ground.
Trees absorb water through their roots and release water vapour through tiny leaf pores (stomata) in a process called transpiration, which absorbs heat energy and cools surrounding air.
Tree roots bind topsoil and reduce rainwater runoff and erosion on school compounds.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Urban foresters and climate scientists in West Africa are studying which native Ghanaian tree species cool towns best while surviving longer dry spells.

investigation.title: Compare Sun and Shade with Two Cups of Water
materials: Clean water from the same bucket or tap
A sunny spot and a shady spot under a tree or veranda
A classroom thermometer (or clean fingers to compare warmth)
steps: Fill both cups halfway with water from the same bucket so they start at the exact same temperature.
Place Cup A out in direct sunlight and Cup B in the shade under a tree for 30 minutes during morning lessons.
After 30 minutes, bring both cups together and measure the water temperature with a thermometer (or touch the outside of each cup to compare).
investigation.whatToNotice: Cup A from the direct sun feels noticeably warmer than Cup B from the shade, showing how shade blocks solar heat energy!
investigation.safetyNote: Use plastic cups (not breakable glass), and stay in the shade as much as possible when setting out and collecting the cups at midday.

factCheck.claim: Trees cool their surroundings both by blocking direct solar radiation (shade) and through evaporative cooling from transpiration.
factCheck.explanation: Canopy shading reduces surface radiant heating, while latent heat of vaporization during leaf transpiration cools ambient air temperature (typically 2–8 °C cooler surface/local feel depending on soil moisture and canopy density).
factCheck.reference: FAO Urban and Peri-Urban Forestry Guidelines; US EPA, Using Trees and Vegetation to Reduce Heat Islands.

pronunciation.guidance: Candidate: "KWAH-meh". English speakers often say "KWAH-mee"; confirm the final vowel.
reviewerNotes: Confirm final vowel (meh vs mee) and the "kw" onset.

characters: Akosua: a ten-year-old Ghanaian girl in Primary 5, wearing a purple-and-white check school dress, neat braided hair with yellow beads, holding a ruler and weather logbook.
Kojo: her ten-year-old classmate, wearing a purple-and-white school shirt and khaki shorts, energetic and quick to guess before measuring.
Mr Boateng: their Primary 5 science teacher who volunteers with the Ghana Meteorological Agency (GMet), wearing a light blue shirt, glasses and carrying a rain gauge cylinder.

teacherGuide.overview: Set in Koforidua in the Eastern Region, this Upper Primary story integrates scientific observation, fair testing, data representation (bar graphs), verified arithmetic (addition, subtraction, and mean of 5-day rainfall data), and the foundational distinction between daily weather and long-term climate across Ghana’s ecological zones.
learningGoals: Explain why a rain gauge must have straight sides and be placed in an open site away from roofs and trees.
Read and interpret a 5-day rainfall dataset in millimetres, calculate the total (50 mm), range (18 mm − 0 mm), and mean (10 mm/day), and represent the data on a bar graph.
Clearly distinguish between daily weather and long-term climate (30+ year averages).
Describe how rainfall records help farmers and water managers in Ghana.

beforeReading: Ask learners: "If a big bucket and a narrow straight jar stand side by side in the open rain, will the water be deeper in the bucket, deeper in the jar, or the same depth?" (Wait to revisit after page 3!)

Pause after page 8 to verify the addition (12 + 0 + 18 + 6 + 14 = 50 mm) and division (50 ÷ 5 = 10 mm).
afterReading: Have every learner draw the 5-day bar graph in their exercise book with a ruler, labelling the horizontal axis (Monday to Friday) and the vertical axis (Rainfall in mm, counting by 2s from 0 to 20).
discussion: Why did Monday’s storm seem bigger to Kojo at first even though Wednesday brought more millimetres of rain?
Why do meteorologists empty the rain gauge at the exact same time every morning after recording the reading?
What is the difference between saying "It rained 18 mm on Wednesday" (weather) and saying "Southern Ghana has its major rainy season from April to July" (climate)?
reflection: When Have you changed your mind about an idea after checking real measurements or facts, just like Kojo did?

mathsExtension.task: Using Akosua’s 5-day data (Monday 12 mm, Tuesday 0 mm, Wednesday 18 mm, Thursday 6 mm, Friday 14 mm), how much rain fell on the first three days combined?
If Saturday had 10 mm of rain, what would be the new total for all 6 days, and what would the 6-day mean be?

support: Use centimetre/millimetre rulers so learners can see how small 1 mm is (one-tenth of a centimetre) and mark 12 mm and 18 mm on paper strips.
stretch: Compare two weeks of rainfall data using a double bar chart and write three sentences comparing their totals and averages.

culturalNotes: The Ghana Meteorological Agency (GMet) operates synoptic and agro-meteorological weather stations across all regions of Ghana.
Akosua, Kojo, and Boateng are Akan names; Koforidua is the regional capital of the Eastern Region.
localiseThis: Discuss whether your school is in the southern bimodal rainfall zone (two wet seasons) or the northern unimodal rainfall zone (one wet season), and when farmers in your community plant maize, yam, or millet.

whatWeKnow: Rainfall depth is measured in millimetres using a standard funnel-and-cylinder rain gauge sited in an unobstructed open area.
Weather describes short-term atmospheric conditions (hours to days), whereas climate describes statistical weather patterns over at least 30 years (WMO standard).
Ghana’s seasonal rainfall is driven by the north-south movement of the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) / West African Monsoon.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Climate scientists at GMet and West African universities are studying how warming oceans in the Gulf of Guinea change the onset dates and intensity of extreme rainfalls for local farmers.

investigation.title: Build a Classroom Rain Gauge and Keep a 5-Day Log
materials: A handful of clean small pebbles or marbles
A plastic ruler marked in millimetres (mm) and waterproof tape
steps: Have the teacher cut the top curved shoulder off the plastic bottle (about one-third from the top).

Place a 3 cm layer of pebbles in the bottom of the bottle to weight it down so wind cannot tip it over, and pour water in just to the top of the pebbles, mark that flat water line as your "0 mm" starting line.
Tape a ruler vertically on the outside of the straight-sided bottle with the "0" mark aligned exactly with your starting water line, then invert the cut top into the bottle as a funnel.

Place the gauge in an open spot outdoors during a rainy week, read how many millimetres the water rises above the 0 line at 8:00 a.m. each morning, refill/reset to the 0 line, and draw a 5-day bar graph!
investigation.whatToNotice: Adding pebbles and filling water to a marked 0 line above the uneven bottle base gives a flat, straight-sided starting level so every millimetre of rain is measured accurately.
investigation.safetyNote: Only the teacher should cut the plastic bottle and smooth any sharp plastic edges with tape; never go outside into an open field during active lightning or thunder, wait until the storm has passed to read the gauge.

factCheck.claim: A standard rain gauge measures precipitation depth in millimetres in an unobstructed open location, and climate is defined over a 30-year baseline.
factCheck.explanation: The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) defines precipitation depth in mm (1 mm = 1 litre per square metre) and uses 30-year climatological standard normals to distinguish climate from daily weather.
factCheck.reference: World Meteorological Organization (WMO) Guide to Instruments and Methods of Observation (WMO-No. 8); Ghana Meteorological Agency (GMet) Educational Resources.

pronunciation.guidance: Candidate: "ah-KOH-swah"; a three-syllable "ah-KOH-soo-ah" may be more accurate.
reviewerNotes: Two or three syllables at the end? Please decide.

teacherGuide.overview: Set at Kakum National Park in the Central Region, this Primary 3–4 story introduces the Kakum Canopy Walkway, rainforest canopy habitats, watershed protection for Cape Coast, the economics and ethics of responsible ecotourism, and the accurate distinction between inscribed UNESCO World Heritage Sites and Ghana’s UNESCO Tentative List.
learningGoals: Explain what ecotourism is and state at least three responsible visitor rules in a national park.
Describe why the canopy walkway allows visitors to observe upper-canopy wildlife without destroying the forest floor.
Explain how Kakum’s rainforest protects the Kakum River watershed that supplies drinking water to Cape Coast.
Understand how tourism revenue and local jobs support conservation.

subjectLinks.subject: Science (Lower/Upper Primary)
subjectLinks.link: Rainforest habitats, water cycle / watersheds, and human impact on ecosystems.

beforeReading: Locate the Central Region, Cape Coast, and Kakum National Park on a map of Ghana.
Ask learners: "If a cousin or friend from another country visited Ghana, what natural place would you be proud to show them, and how would you keep it clean?"
whileReading: Pause after page 4 to note the numbers: 7 bridges, 350 metres total length, up to 40 metres above the forest floor.
Pause after page 8 to trace where visitor money goes (park rangers, trail maintenance, local guides, village artisans).
afterReading: Have learners design a "Welcome to Kakum, Leave Only Footprints" poster listing three rules for visitors.
discussion: Why do more birds and monkeys live high in the rainforest canopy than on the dark forest floor?
How does protecting trees in Kakum help someone turning on a water tap in Cape Coast?
What is the difference between tourism that harms nature (littering, disturbing animals) and ecotourism that protects nature?
reflection: What natural place in your own community, a stream, grove, park, or beach, needs people to care for it the way rangers care for Kakum?

mathsExtension.task: The Kakum Canopy Walkway has 7 bridges with a total length of 350 metres. What is the average length of each bridge if they were equal?
If a school group of 10 children visits the walkway and each child’s ticket is 15 cedis, how much does the group pay in total toward park conservation?

support: Act out the four ecotourism rules from page 2 using simple hand gestures.
stretch: Write a postcard from Jayden to his school in London explaining three things he learned about Ghana’s rainforest.

culturalNotes: Kakum National Park was gazetted as a national park in 1992 and its Canopy Walkway opened in 1995 through collaboration between the Wildlife Division (Forestry Commission), the Ghana Heritage Conservation Trust, and Conservation International.

Accurate heritage note: Ghana’s inscribed UNESCO World Heritage Sites are the Forts and Castles (Volta, Greater Accra, Central and Western Regions, 1979) and the Asante Traditional Buildings (1980). Kakum National Park (Assin Attandanso Reserve) was placed on Ghana’s UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List in 2000.
localiseThis: Connect to the nearest protected forest reserve, wildlife sanctuary, waterfall, or river catchment in your region.

whatWeKnow: Tropical rainforest canopies house the majority of forest biodiversity because sunlight drives flowering and fruiting in the upper tree crowns.
Forested watersheds like Kakum regulate stream flow, filter sediment, and sustain municipal water supplies for Cape Coast and surrounding districts.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Canopy biologists are still cataloging hundreds of insect, orchid, and epiphyte species that live exclusively in the high crowns of West African upper-Guinean rainforests.

investigation.title: See How Forest Roots and Leaves Keep Water Clean
materials: Two cut plastic bottle funnels (or two small flowerpots with drainage holes)
Loose bare soil for Funnel A
Soil covered with dead leaves, grass roots, or moss for Funnel B
steps: Place bare loose soil in Funnel A over Cup A, and soil covered with a thick layer of leaves and roots in Funnel B over Cup B.
Pour the same amount of water slowly over both funnels to imitate rain falling on a bare hill versus a forested Kakum hill.
Compare how muddy or clear the water is in Cup A versus Cup B!
investigation.whatToNotice: The water filtering through the leaves and roots (Funnel B) comes out much clearer and flows more steadily, showing how forest cover protects rivers like the Kakum River!
investigation.safetyNote: Wash hands with soap and clean water after handling soil and leaves, and do not drink the test water.

factCheck.claim: The Kakum Canopy Walkway consists of 7 bridges spanning ~350 metres at heights up to 40 metres, and Kakum is on Ghana’s UNESCO Tentative List while protecting the Kakum River watershed.
factCheck.explanation: Kakum National Park (375 km²) protects the headwaters of the Kakum, Nemimi, and Nbuakosua rivers supplying Cape Coast; it is listed on the UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List (Ref. 1393, submitted 2000).
factCheck.reference: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Kakum National Park (Assin Attandanso Reserve) Tentative List Ref. 1393; Forestry Commission of Ghana (Wildlife Division).

teacherGuide.overview: Framed through a guided visit to the Manhyia Palace Museum in Kumasi, this Primary 5–JHS 1 story presents the verified historical context of Nana Yaa Asantewaa (Queen Mother of Ejisu), the 1896 exile of Asantehene Nana Prempeh I, the sacred meaning of the Golden Stool (Sika Dwa Kofi), Governor Frederick Hodgson’s demand on 28 March 1900, and the 1900 War of the Golden Stool, while explicitly teaching learners how historians distinguish primary records and oral traditions from invented dialogue.
learningGoals: Explain the constitutional role of the Queen Mother (Ohemmaa) in Asante governance and identify Nana Yaa Asantewaa as Queen Mother of Ejisu.
Explain why the Golden Stool (Sika Dwa Kofi) is sacred to the Asante nation and why Governor Hodgson’s demand on 28 March 1900 provoked resistance.
Distinguish between verified historical facts, oral traditions of speeches, and modern museum framing.
Reflect on how courage, sacrifice, and unity protect national dignity.

subjectLinks.link: Colonial rule, resistance movements, Nana Yaa Asantewaa and the 1900 War of the Golden Stool.

subjectLinks.subject: Our World Our People

beforeReading: Locate Kumasi and Ejisu in the Ashanti Region on a map of Ghana, and locate Sierra Leone and the Seychelles on a map of Africa and the Indian Ocean.
Ask learners: "How do we know what happened in Ghana before anyone now living was born?"
whileReading: Pause after page 2 to discuss why historians cross-check multiple sources (written dispatches, photos, and oral traditions).
Pause after page 8 to note why Curator Agyeman explains that Yaa Asantewaa’s speech is preserved in meaning through oral history rather than a tape recording.
afterReading: Create a two-column chart on the board: "Verified Historical Facts (with dates)" and "Lessons on Leadership for Today".
discussion: Why was the Golden Stool never sat upon, and why did Governor Hodgson’s demand show a deep misunderstanding of Asante culture and sovereignty?
What role did women play in leadership and governance in traditional Ghanaian societies as shown by Nana Yaa Asantewaa?
Even though Nana Yaa Asantewaa was eventually captured and exiled to the Seychelles, why do historians consider the defence of the Golden Stool a lasting triumph?
reflection: When is a time in school or community life when standing up for what is right requires quiet courage?

mathsExtension.task: Nana Prempeh I was exiled in 1896 and returned to Kumasi in 1924. How many years was he in exile?
The War of the Golden Stool began in March 1900 and Nana Yaa Asantewaa passed away in the Seychelles in 1921. How many years passed between March 1900 and 1921?

support: Use a visual timeline with four dates: 1896 (Exile of Prempeh I), 28 March 1900 (Hodgson’s demand & Yaa Asantewaa’s leadership), 1921 (Yaa Asantewaa’s passing in Seychelles), and 1924 (Return of Prempeh I).
stretch: Write a short historical essay explaining how comparing British colonial records and Asante oral traditions gives a fuller picture of the 1900 war than reading only one side.

culturalNotes: Nana Yaa Asantewaa (c. 1840–1921) was the Edwesohemmaa (Queen Mother of Ejisu/Edweso). Manhyia Palace Museum in Kumasi preserves royal Asante history and artefacts.
localiseThis: Connect to respected historical leaders (male and female) from your own region or traditional area in Ghana.

whatWeKnow: In 1896 British authorities exiled Asantehene Nana Prempeh I; on 28 March 1900 Governor Sir Frederick Hodgson demanded the Golden Stool at Kumasi.

Nana Yaa Asantewaa, Queen Mother of Ejisu, led the 1900 resistance (War of the Golden Stool); she was later exiled to the Seychelles where she died in October 1921, while the Golden Stool was never captured.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Ghanaian and international historians continue archiving local family oral histories, photographs from the Seychelles exile, and regional accounts of the 1900 stockade defences across Ashanti towns.

investigation.title: Be a Historian: Compare Two Eyewitness Accounts
materials: A short 1-minute classroom action (for example, the teacher walks to the board, draws a star, puts down the chalk, and opens a window)
steps: Have the teacher perform a short 4-step action in front of the class without announcing it beforehand.
Ask three learners sitting in different parts of the room to write down what they saw, and ask a fourth learner to interview them and combine the evidence.
Compare the accounts: which details did every witness agree on, and which details were only visible from one angle?
investigation.whatToNotice: Different witnesses notice different details, so historians compare multiple independent accounts and physical clues to reconstruct what truly happened!

factCheck.reference: Boahen, A. A. (2003). Yaa Asantewaa and the Asante-British War of 1900–1. James Currey / Sub-Saharan Publishers; Arhin, K. (2000). The Role of Yaa Asantewaa in the 1900 Asante War of Resistance; Manhyia Palace Museum Historical Archives.

teacherGuide.overview: Set on a vegetable farm near Dawhenya on the Accra Plains, this Primary 5–6 story teaches the science and economics of tropical greenhouse farming: photosynthesis, rain and pest protection, the critical scientific distinction between a physical greenhouse structure and the planetary atmospheric greenhouse effect, tropical ventilation and humidity management, drip irrigation, integrated pest management, and a verified Ghana cedi farm budget.
learningGoals: Explain how a greenhouse controls growing conditions (sunlight for photosynthesis, shelter from heavy rain, drip irrigation for roots, mesh netting against pests).

Distinguish clearly between how a farm greenhouse traps warm air physically (suppressing convection/wind) and how Earth’s atmospheric greenhouse effect works (gases absorbing and re-emitting infrared radiation).

Explain realistic limitations and trade-offs: poor ventilation causes severe overheating in Ghana’s climate, pests can still enter without strict hygiene, and construction/maintenance costs require careful budgeting.
Calculate total costs (1,000 cedis), revenue (1,600 cedis), and net profit (600 cedis).

Why does drip irrigation save water and reduce leaf diseases compared to splashing water over the whole plant?

whatWeKnow: Physical greenhouses warm primarily by suppressing convective air mixing with the outside atmosphere, whereas the planetary greenhouse effect is driven by radiative absorption and re-emission by greenhouse gases (CO2, H2O, CH4).
In tropical climates, passive roof-and-side ventilation and insect-exclusion netting are essential to keep daytime temperatures below ~32–35 °C where tomato pollen viability drops.
Drip irrigation significantly increases water-use efficiency and reduces foliar fungal pathogens compared to overhead watering.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Agronomists in Ghana are breeding heat-tolerant tomato varieties and testing solar-powered cooling fans and locally made cocopeat growing media to lower greenhouse startup costs for young farmers.

investigation.title: Test How Ventilation Controls Heat in a Mini-Greenhouse
materials: Three identical clear plastic bowls or cut clear plastic bottles
Three small strips of cardboard or soil beds
A sunny windowsill or outdoor table
steps: Place Bowl A upside down completely closed over a cardboard base in the sun (no ventilation).
Place Bowl B upside down with two small gaps propped open at the bottom and a vent hole at the top (ventilated greenhouse), and leave Base C uncovered in the open air.
After 15 minutes in the sun, measure the air temperature inside Bowl A, inside Bowl B, and on open Base C.
investigation.whatToNotice: Closed Bowl A becomes dangerously hot very quickly, while ventilated Bowl B stays sheltered from wind while keeping a moderate temperature closer to the healthy range for plants!
investigation.safetyNote: Teacher should pre-cut any vent holes in plastic bottles; do not leave sealed containers in extreme heat for long periods.

factCheck.claim: A physical greenhouse warms primarily by preventing convective heat loss (trapping warm air), whereas the atmospheric greenhouse effect operates via infrared radiative absorption by greenhouse gases.
factCheck.explanation: As demonstrated by R. W. Wood (1909) and standard atmospheric physics, a physical greenhouse suppresses air convection; atmospheric warming is governed by infrared-active gases.
factCheck.reference: IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) WGI Glossary & FAQ; American Meteorological Society Education Resources.
factCheck.analogyNote: Calling atmospheric warming the "greenhouse effect" is a historical metaphor; teachers should highlight Uncle Ofori’s explanation on pages 5–6 so pupils do not think there is a literal glass roof in the sky.

factCheck.claim: In tropical climates like Ghana, tomato fruit set fails when daytime temperatures exceed ~35–38 °C, making ventilation, drip irrigation, and integrated pest scouting essential.
factCheck.explanation: High heat (>35 °C) impairs pollen germination in Solanum lycopersicum; tropical net-houses require passive ridge ventilation and IPM scouting.
factCheck.reference: FAO (2017). Good Agricultural Practices for Greenhouse Vegetable Production in the Mediterranean and Tropical Regions; CSIR–Crops Research Institute (Ghana) Vegetable Production Guides.

teacherGuide.overview: Set at Cape Coast Castle in the Central Region, this JHS 1–3 history and citizenship story models a respectful, evidence-based educational visit led by the Ghana Museums and Monuments Board (GMMB). It establishes West Africa’s pre-colonial achievements, traces the 1653 Swedish and 1664 British history of the fortress, confronts the injustice of the transatlantic slave trade without graphic sensationalism or invented survivor quotes, explains the symbolic "Door of No Return" / "Door of Return", and connects historical memory to universal human rights.
learningGoals: Explain the historical significance of Cape Coast Castle as an inscribed UNESCO World Heritage Site managed by the Ghana Museums and Monuments Board.
Trace how coastal trade shifted from gold and timber to the transatlantic slave trade linking West Africa, the Americas/Caribbean, and Europe.
Explain why visitors from Ghana, the African diaspora, and around the world visit Cape Coast Castle to remember and reconnect.
Articulate why preserving painful historical evidence protects human rights and dignity today.

beforeReading: Locate Cape Coast in the Central Region on a map of Ghana, and display a world map showing the Atlantic Ocean between West Africa and the Americas.
Establish a respectful classroom norm: we study this history quietly and seriously because it involves real human beings and families.
whileReading: Pause after page 3 to emphasize that West African societies had advanced metallurgy, agriculture, gold trade, and governance long before European ships arrived.

Pause after page 10 to discuss the meaning of both sides of the portal: "Door of No Return" (historical reality of forced departure) and "Door of Return" (1998 Emancipation Day welcome to the diaspora).
afterReading: Discuss Esi’s closing sentence on page 12: how does remembering past injustice help us protect freedom and human rights today?
discussion: Why did Mr Mensah point out the architectural contrast between the dark lower chambers and the airy governor’s rooms and chapel directly above?
Why do descendants of enslaved Africans in the Americas and the Caribbean travel thousands of kilometres to stand inside Cape Coast and Elmina Castles?
How can young Ghanaians welcome diaspora visitors while also protecting and maintaining Ghana’s historical monuments?
reflection: What does the word "dignity" mean to you in how we treat classmates, strangers, and people from every background?

mathsExtension.task: The Swedish timber fort Carolusborg was built at Cape Coast in 1653, and Cape Coast Castle was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1979. How many years passed between 1653 and 1979?

culturalNotes: Cape Coast Castle (along with Elmina Castle and other coastal fortifications) was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1979 under "Forts and Castles, Volta, Greater Accra, Central and Western Regions" and is conserved by the Ghana Museums and Monuments Board (GMMB).
Avoid role-playing or dramatising the suffering of enslaved captives in class; keep all activities analytical, empathetic, and respectful.
localiseThis: Connect to any historical monuments, museums, or heritage sites preserved by the Ghana Museums and Monuments Board in your region.

whatWeKnow: Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1979, Cape Coast Castle grew from a 1555 Portuguese lodge and 1653 Swedish fort (Carolusborg) into the British headquarters on the Gold Coast (1664–1877) and a major holding fortress of the transatlantic slave trade.
Historians estimate that over 12.5 million African men, women, and children were forced onto transatlantic slave ships between the 16th and 19th centuries.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Archaeologists, historians, and geneticists in Ghana and the diaspora continue researching archival shipping manifests, oral histories along inland slave routes (such as Assin Manso and Salaga), and conservation methods to protect coastal stone monuments from sea-level rise and salt erosion.

investigation.title: Heritage Conservation Observation: How Salt Air Affects Stone and Metal
materials: Two small pieces of chalk or porous limestone/brick
Two small iron nails (clean, handled carefully)
Two shallow dishes: Dish A with plain tap water, Dish B with salty water (1 spoon of salt stirred in)
steps: Place one piece of chalk/stone and one nail in Dish A (fresh water) and the second pair in Dish B (salt water), then lift them onto paper towels to dry in the air each day for 3 days.
Observe how salt crystals form inside the pores of the chalk/stone as water evaporates and how salt speeds up rust on iron.
investigation.whatToNotice: Salt water and sea spray speed up rusting and leave salt crystals that weather porous stone and lime mortar, showing why GMMB conservators must work continually to preserve coastal monuments like Cape Coast Castle!
investigation.safetyNote: Wash hands after handling rusty nails or salt solutions, and dispose of rusted nails safely with the teacher.

factCheck.claim: Cape Coast Castle was expanded as Carolusborg by the Swedes in 1653, taken by the British in 1664, and inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979 under the stewardship of the Ghana Museums and Monuments Board.
factCheck.explanation: Historical and architectural documentation by GMMB and UNESCO World Heritage Convention (Ref. 34) confirm the 1653 Swedish construction under Heinrich Caarlof, 1664 British capture, and 1979 UNESCO inscription.
factCheck.reference: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Forts and Castles, Volta, Greater Accra, Central and Western Regions (Ref. 34); Anquandah, J. (1999). Castles & Forts of Ghana. Ghana Museums and Monuments Board; Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database (SlaveVoyages.org).

investigation.title: One Basket vs Three Baskets Simulation
materials: Ten counters (representing 100 cedis each = 1,000 cedis), three cups labelled Stock A, Stock B, and Bond, and a coin to flip.
steps: Scenario 1 (Undiversified): Put all 10 counters (1,000 cedis) into Stock B alone. When Stock B drops by 10%, calculate your ending total (900 cedis, a 100-cedi loss).
Scenario 2 (Diversified): Place 4 counters in Stock A (+12.5% → 450 cedis), 2 counters in Stock B (-10% → 180 cedis), and 4 counters in Bond (+15% → 460 cedis).
Add the three cups in Scenario 2 (450 + 180 + 460 = 1,090 cedis) and compare with Scenario 1.
investigation.safetyNote: Conduct under adult supervision.

teacherGuide.overview: An upper-primary and JHS 1 financial literacy story that uses the vivid metaphor of "buying an umbrella before the rain" to explain risk pooling, premiums, claims, deductibles, policy conditions/exclusions, Ghana’s National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS), regulation by the National Insurance Commission (NIC), and why families need both emergency savings and insurance.
learningGoals: Explain how risk pooling spreads the cost of rare, expensive disasters across many contributors (100 × 100 = 10,000 cedis pool).
Define premium, policy, claim, deductible and exclusions accurately.
Calculate an insurance payout after subtracting a deductible (2,000 − 200 = 1,800 cedis).
Identify the National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS) and the National Insurance Commission (NIC) in Ghana.

investigation.title: Risk-Pooling Dice Simulation
materials: Six groups of pupils, one 6-sided die, and 60 counters (10 counters per group).
steps: Round 1 (No Insurance Pool): Each group keeps its 10 counters. Roll the die, whichever group number is rolled suffers a "storm loss" of 12 counters (more than they have!).
Round 2 (Risk Pool): Each of the 6 groups contributes 3 counters (premium) into a central Umbrella Pool (6 × 3 = 18 counters in the pool, leaving 7 counters per group).
Roll the die for the storm loss of 12 counters: the Umbrella Pool pays 11 counters and the affected group pays a 1-counter deductible, every group stays afloat!

whatWeKnow: Under Ghana’s National Pensions Act, 2008 (Act 766), the National Pensions Regulatory Authority (NPRA) regulates a Three-Tier system: Tier 1 (SSNIT mandatory basic national social security), Tier 2 (mandatory privately managed occupational scheme), and Tier 3 (voluntary provident fund and personal pension schemes designed to include informal-sector workers).
Compound growth follows the formula A = P(1 + r)^t, meaning time in the market exponentially increases the effect of reinvested returns.

investigation.title: Year-by-Year Compounding Seed Lab
materials: 100 dried beans or maize kernels and 3 small bowls labelled "Start (Year 0)", "End of Year 1", and "End of Year 2".
steps: Count 100 beans into the Year 0 bowl (representing 1,000 cedis, where 1 bean = 10 cedis).
For Year 1 at 10% growth, add 10% of 100 beans (10 beans) to get 110 beans (1,100 cedis).
For Year 2 at 10% growth, calculate 10% of the 110 beans (11 beans) and add them to get 121 beans (1,210 cedis). Point out the 11th bean that came from Year 1’s growth!

investigation.title: Paper-Prototype Usability Test
materials: Two sheets of paper, a pencil, and a classmate who has not seen your drawing.
steps: On Sheet A, draw a cluttered "Version 1" phone screen with 12 tiny buttons and long paragraphs. On Sheet B, draw a clean "Version 2" screen with 3 clear choices.
Show Sheet A to your partner for 5 seconds and ask them how they would book an electrician. Time how long it takes them to find the right button.
Repeat with Sheet B and compare which design was faster, clearer, and needed less explanation.

investigation.title: Cost-Per-Day Civic Maths Check
materials: Exercise book, pencil, and a basic calculator.
steps: Write down the length of a four-year local term in days: 4 × 365 = 1,460 days.
Divide a 50-cedi election handout by 1,460 days (50 ÷ 1,460 ≈ 0.034 cedis, or about 3.4 pesewas per day).
Now compare that 3.4 pesewas per day with the value of clean borehole water and a dry clinic roof serving 5,000 residents every day for 1,460 days.

teacherGuide.overview: An upper-primary and JHS environmental science and citizenship story examining the ecological, health and economic impacts of destructive illegal mining (galamsey) on Ghana’s rivers. It teaches the rigorous scientific distinction between visible turbidity and laboratory-verified chemical contamination, strict child safety around polluted water, and how law enforcement must be paired with sustainable youth livelihoods and land reclamation.
learningGoals: Explain how high turbidity and suspended sediment harm aquatic ecosystems (blocking sunlight for photosynthesis, clogging fish gills, silting riverbeds) and raise water-treatment costs.
Distinguish between visible evidence of sediment pollution and laboratory-confirmed identification of chemical contaminants such as mercury.
Follow strict safety rules: never touch, wade into, or sample polluted water without professional adult supervision and protective equipment.
Explain how environmental protection, lawful governance (EPA Ghana, Water Resources Commission) and sustainable youth employment work together.

whatWeKnow: High turbidity from alluvial mining strips riverbank topsoil, blocks light needed by aquatic primary producers, smothers benthic habitats, and severely increases coagulant (alum) demand and pump wear at Ghana Water Limited treatment plants.

Dissolved or trace heavy metals (such as mercury or arsenic) cannot be identified by visual colour alone; confirmation requires certified analytical chemistry methods (such as atomic absorption spectroscopy).
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Ghanaian environmental scientists and soil engineers are researching phytoremediation (using specialised plants and biochar) to help rehabilitate degraded mining soils faster.

investigation.title: Safe Classroom Torch & Turbidity Test
materials: Two clear plastic cups of clean tap water, one teaspoon of clean dry garden soil, a white card, and a small torch (never use polluted river water!).
steps: Leave Cup A filled with clear tap water. Stir one teaspoon of clean garden soil into Cup B to simulate suspended sediment.
Hold the white card behind Cup A and shine the torch through the side, notice how bright the light is on the card.
Shine the torch through Cup B, notice how the suspended soil scatters and blocks the light beam, just as turbid water blocks sunlight from underwater plants.

Treat both migrants and local workers with dignity and respect.

teacherGuide.overview: A Primary 6 to JHS 2 history, physics and civic-engineering story set on a fictional school excursion to the Akosombo Dam. Learners trace energy transformations in hydroelectricity, calculate station output, and examine the real historical benefits, human resettlement (80,000 people across 700+ villages) and ecological impacts of the Volta River Project.
learningGoals: Trace the four-stage energy conversion in a hydroelectric station: gravitational potential → kinetic → mechanical → electrical energy.
Explain how spinning magnets inside copper coils induce an electric current (Faraday’s electromagnetic induction).
Calculate total power output across multiple generating units (6 × 170 MW = 1,020 MW).
Evaluate both the national industrial benefits and the human/environmental trade-offs (displacement of ~80,000 people, schistosomiasis, downstream flow changes) of the Volta River Project.

Why is hydroelectricity considered a renewable energy source, and why does Ghana today combine hydropower with solar and thermal power?

whatWeKnow: The Akosombo Dam was constructed between 1961 and 1965 and officially inaugurated in January 1966, creating Lake Volta (~8,502 km² surface area).
Hydroelectric stations convert gravitational potential energy of elevated water into kinetic energy, mechanical turbine rotation, and electrical energy via electromagnetic induction.
Formation of Lake Volta required resettling approximately 80,000 people from over 700 villages into 52 resettlement towns and altered aquatic and downstream ecosystems.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Energy engineers are researching how floating solar photovoltaics (floatovoltaics) on reservoirs can generate extra power while reducing water evaporation during hot dry seasons.
Ecologists and hydrologists continue studying how environmental flow releases from dams can best restore downstream river habitats and livelihoods.

investigation.title: Build a Simple Classroom Waterwheel Turbine
materials: A clean plastic bottle cap or small cardboard disc coated in tape
6 small pieces of stiff plastic cut from a yoghurt cup (for blades)
A wooden skewer or pencil (as the shaft)
A plastic jug of water and a bucket to catch the water
steps: Slot or tape the 6 small plastic blades evenly around the rim of the bottle cap to form a miniature turbine wheel, and push the wooden skewer through the centre.
Hold the skewer loosely with two fingers over an empty bucket and pour water steadily from the jug onto the side blades from 10 cm above.
Now pour the water from 30 cm above the wheel and compare how fast the wheel spins.
investigation.whatToNotice: Pouring water from a greater height gives the water more gravitational potential energy, which turns into faster kinetic motion and spins the turbine wheel faster, just like the high water level above the Akosombo penstocks!
investigation.safetyNote: Use blunt scissors under adult supervision and perform the pouring test over a bucket or outdoors so the floor stays dry.

teacherGuide.overview: A JHS 1–3 artificial intelligence, computer vision and agricultural entrepreneurship story set in Techiman. Learners discover how machine-learning models learn from training data, why unrepresentative studio datasets fail in real Ghanaian farm conditions, why separate test sets and farmer privacy/consent matter, and why AI must support, never replace, human experts.
learningGoals: Explain how a supervised machine-learning model learns patterns from labelled training data and is evaluated on unseen test data.
Distinguish between a false positive (flagging a healthy dusty leaf as diseased) and a false negative (missing a truly diseased leaf in shadow).
Calculate model accuracy rates from test counts (9/20 = 45% vs 180/200 = 90%).
Explain why data privacy, informed consent and human-in-the-loop oversight are essential in AI engineering.

beforeReading: Ask learners: "How do you recognise the difference between a ripe mango and an unripe mango? How would you teach a computer that has never seen a mango to tell the difference?"
whileReading: Pause at page 5 and calculate the percentage: 9 correct out of 20 plots = (9 ÷ 20) × 100 = 45%.
Pause at page 7 to discuss why flying a camera over farms requires clear privacy rules and neighbour consent.
afterReading: Run the classroom "Paper-Leaf Classifier" game so students experience how a limited training set leads to misclassification.
discussion: Why did a model with 90% accuracy on studio photos fail on Uncle Kwabena’s farm?
What would happen if a farmer sprayed expensive pesticide every time an unverified AI app gave a false positive?
Why did Tariq say testing a model on its own training images is like giving a student the exam questions before the test?
reflection: What Would You Build, Discover or Change? What real problem in your community could a sensor, app or tool help solve, and which human experts would you partner with?

mathsExtension.task: In the first field trial, Mansa’s model tested 20 plots and got 9 right. What percentage was correct, and what percentage was misclassified?
In the second trial, the retrained model was tested on 200 unseen field images and classified 180 correctly. What was its accuracy percentage, and how many images did it still misclassify?
mathsExtension.answer: Accuracy: (180 ÷ 200) × 100 = 90%. Misclassified: 200 − 180 = 20 images (10%), showing why human verification is still needed.

support: Focus on the everyday meaning of "training examples", "false alarm (false positive)" and "missed problem (false negative)".
stretch: Design a simple confusion matrix (2×2 table of Actual Healthy / Actual Diseased vs Predicted Healthy / Predicted Diseased) using the 20 plots from Page 5 (9 correct, 8 false positives, 3 false negatives).

culturalNotes: Techiman in the Bono East Region is one of West Africa’s major agricultural market hubs, bringing together farmers and traders from across Ghana.
localiseThis: Substitute the main crop grown around your school (e.g., cassava mosaic disease, cocoa black pod, millet, or tomato blight).

whatWeKnow: Supervised image-classification models learn statistical patterns from labelled training images and often fail ("domain shift" or dataset bias) when deployed in lighting, soil or weather conditions absent from their training set.
Separating training data from an independent hold-out test set is required to measure how well a model generalises to unseen data.
Agricultural AI tools work best as decision-support systems paired with human agronomists and farmers rather than autonomous chemical-spraying triggers.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Computer-vision researchers in Ghana and across Africa are developing lightweight edge-AI models that can run offline on low-cost smartphones without needing mobile internet in remote farms.

investigation.title: Spot Training-Data Bias with a Classroom Sorting Game
materials: 10 index cards or slips of paper with drawings of leaves
steps: Have Group A create 6 "Training Cards": draw 3 healthy green round leaves and 3 diseased yellow pointed leaves. Show ONLY these 6 cards to Group B and ask Group B to write down the rule for spotting a diseased leaf.
Now hand Group B 4 "Real Farm Test Cards" that include a healthy pointed green leaf with a tiny brown soil speck and a round leaf with yellow disease spots.
Check whether Group B’s rule misclassified the pointed healthy leaf or the round diseased leaf, and discuss how adding more varied training cards fixes the rule.
investigation.whatToNotice: When the training cards only showed one leaf shape or lacked soil specks, the rule learned the wrong shortcut, just like Mansa’s first AI model!
investigation.safetyNote: Standard classroom paper activity; no special hazards.

factCheck.claim: Machine-learning image classifiers trained on laboratory leaf images (such as PlantVillage studio photos) often drop sharply in accuracy when tested on real field images unless retrained on diverse field data.
factCheck.explanation: Peer-reviewed agricultural computer-vision studies show models achieving >90% accuracy on uniform-background lab datasets frequently drop below 50% on real field photos due to background clutter, illumination variance and dust.
factCheck.reference: Mohanty et al. (2016), Frontiers in Plant Science; Ferentinos (2018), Computers and Electronics in Agriculture.

teacherGuide.overview: A Primary 4–6 agricultural science, trade and entrepreneurship story following a cocoa bean from a sustainable shaded farm in Sefwi Wiawso to a Ghanaian chocolate factory in Tema. Learners explore fermentation chemistry, post-harvest quality control, cocoa processing (nibs, liquor, butter, powder, conching), child-safe farming standards, and the economics of value addition.
learningGoals: Describe the post-harvest science of cocoa on the farm: 6-day fermentation and 7–10-day sun-drying to under 8% moisture.
Trace factory processing from roasted beans to cocoa nibs, cocoa liquor, cocoa butter, cocoa powder and conched chocolate.
Distinguish gross retail revenue from net profit using an illustrative value-addition cost breakdown.
Explain why sustainable shade-tree agroforestry and strict child-safe farm rules protect Ghana’s cocoa heritage.

beforeReading: Show learners a picture of a cocoa pod and a bar of Ghanaian chocolate (or cocoa powder) and ask: "What steps happen between the tree and the tin?"
Note that the financial numbers on pages 8–9 are illustrative classroom examples designed to teach cost vs profit arithmetic, as real market prices change over time.
whileReading: Pause after page 4 to ask why unfermented cocoa beans do not taste like chocolate even if you roast them.
Pause after page 9 to work through the cost table on the board: 300 cedis (beans) + 700 cedis (other inputs, wages, energy, packaging) = 1,000 cedis total cost.
afterReading: Have learners pick another Ghanaian crop (cassava, shea nuts, mango, groundnuts, tiger nuts) and draw a 4-step "Raw to Value-Added Product" poster.
discussion: Why do shade trees help a cocoa farm stay healthy for many years?
Why is it wrong to assume that the entire price difference between raw cocoa beans and a retail chocolate bar is pure profit?
What new jobs are created in Ghana when cocoa is processed into butter, powder, cosmetics and chocolate bars locally?
reflection: What Would You Build, Discover or Change? Choose one crop grown in your region, what new snack, drink or household product could you make from it, and how would you package it cleanly?

mathsExtension.task: In the illustrative workshop example, 100 chocolate bars sell for 12 cedis each (1,200 cedis total revenue). Raw cocoa beans cost 300 cedis and processing, ingredients, wages and packaging cost 700 cedis. What is the net profit per bar?
mathsExtension.answer: Total profit = 1,200 − (300 + 700) = 200 cedis. Profit per bar = 200 ÷ 100 = 2 cedis per bar.

mathsExtension.task: If a cooperative dries 500 kg of wet fermented beans and loses 55% of the weight as water evaporates during sun-drying, how many kilograms of dry cocoa beans remain?
mathsExtension.answer: Water lost = 55% of 500 = 275 kg. Dry beans remaining = 500 − 275 = 225 kg (45% of 500 kg).

support: Create a simple 5-card picture sequence: Pod → White Beans → Brown Dried Beans → Cocoa Liquor/Butter → Chocolate Bar.
stretch: Investigate how by-products of the cocoa pod (such as cocoa pod husks and mucilage sweatings) are used in Ghana to make potash black soap (alata samina) and fruit juice.

culturalNotes: Since Tetteh Quarshie introduced Amelonado cocoa pods to Akuapem Mampong in 1879, cocoa has been central to Ghanaian rural livelihoods and national pride.
localiseThis: In northern coastal or savannah zones where cocoa does not grow, compare the cocoa value chain with the shea butter (Vitellaria paradoxa) or cashew value chain.

whatWeKnow: Cocoa flowers and pods grow directly on the trunk and older branches (cauliflory) and are pollinated primarily by tiny biting midges (Forcipomyia) that thrive in moist shaded leaf litter.
Microbial fermentation (yeasts, lactic acid bacteria and acetic acid bacteria) over ~6 days and sun-drying to ~7.5% moisture are essential to develop chocolate flavour precursors and prevent mould.
Roasting, winnowing, grinding into cocoa liquor, hydraulic pressing into butter and cake, and conching are the core industrial steps of chocolate manufacturing.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Food scientists at the Cocoa Research Institute of Ghana (CRIG) continue researching new value-added products from cocoa pulp, husks and flavanol-rich extracts.

investigation.title: Observe How Fat (Cocoa Butter) and Solids Behave in Warm Water
materials: 2 cups of warm water and 1 spoonful of cooking oil or shea/cocoa butter
Two clear cups and a spoon
steps: In Cup A, stir a spoonful of cocoa powder into warm water and observe how the fine solid particles suspend in the liquid.
In Cup B, add a small drop of oil or melted shea/cocoa butter to warm water and observe how pure plant fats separate unless mixed and emulsified.
Discuss how pressing cocoa liquor separates the fat (cocoa butter) from the dry solids (cocoa powder).
investigation.whatToNotice: Cocoa beans contain both natural fat (cocoa butter) and dry cocoa solids; separating or recombining them in precise ratios lets food scientists make either drinkable cocoa powder or smooth solid chocolate!
investigation.safetyNote: Use warm tap water (never boiling water) under teacher supervision.

factCheck.claim: Ghanaian cocoa beans undergo ~6 days of heap or tray fermentation followed by sun-drying to ~7.5% moisture before quality grading.
factCheck.explanation: Standard Ghana Cocoa Board (COCOBOD) and CRIG post-harvest protocols specify 6 days of fermentation with turning and 7–10 days of sun-drying to ~7.5% moisture content.
factCheck.reference: Cocoa Research Institute of Ghana (CRIG) Farmers’ Handbook on Cocoa Production.

teacherGuide.overview: A Primary 2–4 biodiversity, pollination and insect-navigation story set in a school garden near Aburi. Learners discover how butterflies use compound eyes (including ultraviolet vision), antennae and foot taste receptors, distinguish local habitat navigation from long-distance migration, and separate established biology from open neuroscience questions.
learningGoals: Describe how a butterfly uses its compound eyes, antennae, proboscis and feet to find and feed on flowers.
Explain how butterflies pollinate flowers while sipping nectar.
Explain that not all butterfly species migrate long distances; many Ghanaian butterflies navigate locally using sun position, scents and landmarks.
Distinguish what biologists already know about insect senses from what scientists are still discovering about tiny insect brains.

Remind learners of the golden rule: we never catch, pinch or touch butterflies’ wings because the tiny scales rub off.
whileReading: Pause at page 5 and ask learners to point to their own noses and tongues, then compare where a butterfly smells (antennae) and tastes (feet).
Pause at page 7 to emphasise why scientists do not assume every butterfly acts like one famous species in another country.

mathsExtension.task: Nhyira and Kojo counted 6 yellow grass butterflies, 4 black-and-yellow swallowtails and 5 white butterflies in 15 minutes. How many butterflies did they count altogether, and how many more yellow grass butterflies than swallowtails did they see?
mathsExtension.answer: Total = 6 + 4 + 5 = 15 butterflies. Difference = 6 − 4 = 2 more yellow grass butterflies than swallowtails.

support: Act out the four butterfly parts with hand gestures: unrolling proboscis (curled finger), antennae (two fingers above head), compound eyes (hands around eyes) and tasting feet (tapping toes).
stretch: Draw a simple bar chart comparing the 3 butterfly groups tallied on Page 8 (6 yellow, 4 swallowtail, 5 white).

culturalNotes: Aburi in the Akuapem South Municipality (Eastern Region) is home to the historic Aburi Botanical Gardens, famous for its rich plant and butterfly diversity.
localiseThis: Observe whatever pollinators visit flowers around your school, butterflies, honeybees, carpenter bees or sunbirds.

whatWeKnow: Butterflies see colour and ultraviolet light patterns with their compound eyes, detect airborne odours with their antennae, taste host-plant chemicals with receptors on their feet (tarsi), and sip liquid through a coiled proboscis.

Ghana has over 900 recorded butterfly species; unlike the North American monarch’s multi-generational continental migration, most Ghanaian species navigate locally or shift seasonally within West African habitats.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Neurobiologists are still investigating the exact neural circuits in the insect central complex that combine sun-compass cues, visual landmarks and odour plumes into spatial memory.

investigation.title: 10-Minute Quiet Pollinator Tally in the Schoolyard
materials: A notebook or sheet of paper ruled into 3 columns (Butterfly / Bee / Other Insect)
A flowering bush or garden patch on the school compound
steps: Stand two steps back from a sunny flowering bush so you do not cast a shadow over the flowers or disturb visiting insects.
For 10 minutes, stay quiet and make one tally mark each time a butterfly, bee or other insect lands on a flower.
Add up the tally marks in each column and compare which flower colour received the most visits.
investigation.whatToNotice: Staying still and quiet lets pollinators behave naturally, and different insects often prefer different flower shapes and colours!
investigation.safetyNote: Never touch, swat at or trap bees, wasps or butterflies; learners with insect-sting allergies should observe from a safe paved walkway with the teacher.

factCheck.claim: Ghana has over 900 butterfly species, and citrus swallowtails (Papilio demodocus) are common across Ghanaian gardens and farms.
factCheck.explanation: Torben Larsen’s Butterflies of West Africa documents over 900 butterfly species in Ghana, with Papilio demodocus widespread wherever citrus and garden flowers grow.
factCheck.reference: Larsen, T. B. (2005). Butterflies of West Africa; Ghana Wildlife Society.

teacherGuide.overview: A Primary 6 to JHS 2 financial-literacy and mathematics story set in Ho. Learners work through exact Ghana cedi calculations comparing simple and compound interest over 3 years (1,000 → 1,100 → 1,210 → 1,331 cedis), understand inflation and debt compounding, and learn how to spot unlicensed get-rich-quick Ponzi scams.
learningGoals: Calculate multi-year simple interest and compound interest in Ghana cedis and explain why compounding grows faster over time.
Explain how inflation reduces the purchasing power of idle cash.
Explain that compounding also applies to unpaid debt, making high-interest loans grow rapidly.
Identify warning signs of financial fraud (unusually high "guaranteed" returns, pressure to act fast, lack of Bank of Ghana or SEC Ghana licensing).
