beforeReading: Ask learners: "If someone offered you 1,000 cedis plus 100 cedis every year (simple), or 1,000 cedis growing by 10% of the new total each year (compound), which would be bigger after 3 years?"
whileReading: Have every learner write down the Year 1 (1,100), Year 2 (1,210) and Year 3 (1,331) calculations in their own notebook alongside Afia on pages 4–6.
Pause at page 8 to discuss why scammers use urgency ("today only!") and greed ("double in 7 days!") to trick people.
afterReading: Compare the 3-year table of Simple vs Compound interest on the chalkboard and compute Year 4 together (1,331 + 133.10 = 1,464.10 cedis).
discussion: Why is keeping all long-term savings in a box at home risky both physically and economically (inflation)?
How does compound interest hurt a borrower who takes a high-interest loan and misses payments?
What two Ghanaian regulatory bodies license banks and investment firms? (Bank of Ghana and the Securities and Exchange Commission, SEC Ghana.)
reflection: What Would You Build, Discover or Change? What is one educational or enterprise goal you want to save for over the next three years, and what rule will protect your family from financial scams?

mathsExtension.task: Calculate the difference after 3 years between 1,000 cedis at 10% simple interest per year and 1,000 cedis at 10% annual compound interest.
mathsExtension.answer: Simple interest after 3 years: 1,000 + (3 × 100) = 1,300 cedis. Compound interest after 3 years: 1,331 cedis. Difference: 1,331 − 1,300 = 31 cedis.

mathsExtension.task: Continue Afia’s 10% compound interest table for one more year (Year 4), starting from the Year 3 balance of 1,331 cedis.

support: Use counters or paper strips of 100 cedis to model Year 1 (10 strips + 1 strip = 11 strips) and Year 2 (11 strips + 1.1 strips = 12.1 strips).
stretch: Calculate what happens if someone borrows 1,000 cedis from an unlicensed lender charging 20% compound interest per month and makes no payments for 2 months (Month 1: 1,200 cedis; Month 2: 1,200 + 240 = 1,440 cedis).

culturalNotes: Ho is the capital of the Volta Region; Yao (Ewe for a boy born on Thursday) and Afia / Akua (Akan day names for Friday / Wednesday) reflect everyday Ghanaian family life.
localiseThis: Point out regulated rural and community banks, credit unions, and Bank of Ghana / SEC Ghana public advisories in your area.

whatWeKnow: Compound growth follows the mathematical formula A = P(1 + r)^n, where interest earned in each period is added to the principal for the next period.
Inflation erodes the real purchasing power of uninvested cash whenever the inflation rate exceeds 0%.
Under Ghanaian law, deposit-taking institutions are regulated by the Bank of Ghana (BoG) and capital-market investment schemes by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Ghana.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Behavioural economists continue researching how youth financial-literacy education and visual compounding tools improve long-term household savings habits.

investigation.title: Build a Visual Staircase of Simple vs Compound Growth
materials: Two coloured pencils (blue for Simple Interest, green for Compound Interest)
steps: Let 1 grid square equal 10 cedis (so 1,000 cedis = 100 squares, or draw bars to scale where 1 cm = 100 cedis).
Draw pairs of bars for Year 0 (1,000 vs 1,000), Year 1 (1,100 vs 1,100), Year 2 (1,200 vs 1,210), Year 3 (1,300 vs 1,331) and Year 4 (1,400 vs 1,464.10).
Shade the extra "interest-on-interest" top section of each green Compound bar and notice how that shaded section grows wider every year.
investigation.whatToNotice: In Year 1 the two bars are equal, but in every year after Year 1 the compound bar pulls further ahead because each year’s interest starts earning its own interest!
investigation.safetyNote: Standard classroom graphing activity; no special safety hazards.

factCheck.claim: 1,000 cedis compounded annually at 10% grows to 1,100 cedis in Year 1, 1,210 cedis in Year 2, and 1,331 cedis in Year 3.
factCheck.reference: Standard compound-interest mathematics: A = P(1 + r)^n.

factCheck.claim: Unusually high "guaranteed" short-term investment returns are a primary red flag of Ponzi and financial fraud schemes.
factCheck.explanation: Both the Bank of Ghana and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Ghana warn citizens that legitimate investments carry risk and that schemes promising guaranteed rapid doubling of money are fraudulent.
factCheck.reference: Bank of Ghana & SEC Ghana Public Investor Protection Advisories.

teacherGuide.overview: A Primary 5 to JHS 1 science, civic-leadership and values story set in the fictional village of Nsuom. Learners see how faith in God inspires unity, diligence and service alongside scientific hydrogeology, strict water-safety rules (why classroom filters never make water drinkable), laboratory testing, transparent public budgeting and preventive maintenance.
learningGoals: Explain why a simple sand-and-cloth filter only removes visible sediment and NEVER removes microscopic pathogens or dissolved chemicals.
Describe how groundwater is stored in underground aquifers and why boreholes must be sited uphill from latrines, sealed and laboratory-tested.
Calculate multi-step community project budgets (200 households × 15 cedis × 12 months = 36,000 cedis + 64,000 grant = 100,000 cedis).
Explain how faith-inspired values, interfaith unity, scientific expertise and transparent public accounting work together to solve community problems.

Why did Engineer Asante refuse to let anyone drink the clear borehole water until the laboratory certificate arrived?

mathsExtension.task: Nsuom puts 500 cedis per month into a bank maintenance account. After 24 months (2 years), how much has been saved, and if a replacement solar pump controller costs 4,200 cedis, how much remains in the maintenance fund after paying for the repair?
mathsExtension.answer: Saved in 24 months: 500 × 24 = 12,000 cedis. Remaining after repair: 12,000 − 4,200 = 7,800 cedis.

mathsExtension.task: In the 100,000-cedi borehole project, the grant covered 64,000 cedis and the community raised 36,000 cedis. What percentage of the total cost did the community raise?

culturalNotes: In Ghanaian towns and villages, Water and Sanitation Management Teams (WSMTs) work with traditional authorities, Assembly Members and diverse religious communities to manage rural water systems.
localiseThis: Discuss where your school’s drinking and handwashing water comes from (GWCL pipe, CWSA borehole, sachet water, rainwater harvesting) and how it is kept safe.

whatWeKnow: Simple mechanical filtration through gravel, sand and cloth removes suspended turbidity (sediment) but does NOT remove dissolved chemicals or microscopic pathogens (bacteria, viruses, protozoa).

Safe rural drinking-water engineering requires hydrogeological siting, sanitary borehole sealing, accredited laboratory testing (microbiological and physicochemical under GSA GS 175 / WHO guidelines) and residual disinfection.
Dedicated community maintenance funds and trained local technicians dramatically reduce rural borehole downtime.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Hydrogeologists in Ghana use satellite remote sensing and geophysical mapping to chart deep Basement Complex fracture aquifers resilient to multi-year droughts.

investigation.title: See Why Sediment Filtration Is Only Step One (Non-Drinkable Demo)
materials: A clear plastic bottle with the bottom cut off by the teacher
Clean pebbles, coarse sand, fine sand and a piece of clean cotton cloth
A jar of muddy water mixed with a drop of safe food colouring (to represent dissolved substances)
steps: Have the teacher secure the cloth over the bottle neck and layer pebbles, coarse sand and fine sand inside to model how soil layers trap large dirt particles.
Pour the muddy coloured water through the sand layers into a clear cup below.
Observe that while the brown mud particles are trapped by the sand, the food colouring (and any invisible microbes) passes right through into the cup!
investigation.whatToNotice: The coloured water in the bottom cup proves that even when big mud particles are filtered out, dissolved substances and microscopic germs pass straight through, which is why classroom-filtered water must NEVER be drunk!
investigation.safetyNote: STRICT SAFETY RULE: Label the cup "DO NOT DRINK, SCIENCE DEMO ONLY" and pour the water on outdoor plants after the demonstration; wash hands with soap and safe running water.

factCheck.claim: A simple sand-and-cloth filter removes suspended sediment but does not make water microbiologically or chemically safe to drink.
factCheck.explanation: Pore spaces in simple sand and cloth filters (typically >10–50 micrometres) are far larger than bacteria (~0.5–5 micrometres), viruses (~0.02–0.3 micrometres) and dissolved ions (fluoride, arsenic, nitrates), requiring disinfection and laboratory verification.
factCheck.reference: World Health Organization (WHO) Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality; Ghana Standards Authority GS 175.

pronunciation.guidance: Candidate: "KWAH-meh". English speakers often say "KWAH-mee"; confirm the final vowel.

Identify factors that can contribute to coastal change, including waves, currents, storms and rising sea level, while recognising the need for local investigation.
Evaluate why dumping rubbish on the beach is harmful and why coastal protection requires scientific assessment and community planning.

investigation.title: Supervised Classroom Sand-and-Water Tray Demonstration
materials: A shallow plastic or metal tray
steps: Shape clean sand at one end of the shallow tray to model a gentle beach slope.
Pour water carefully into the other end of the tray.
Gently tilt or wave a ruler in the water and observe how grains of sand shift and move.
investigation.whatToNotice: Moving water picks up and transports sand grains (sediment), changing the shape of the model shoreline.
investigation.safetyNote: Conduct inside the classroom under teacher supervision. Never take children near unstable cliffs, dangerous surf or eroding coastal structures.

factCheck.claim: Waves, currents, storms and changes in sea level can affect coastlines, and local conditions must be investigated.
factCheck.explanation: Coastal morphodynamics depend on wave energy, longshore currents, sediment supply, human activities and relative sea-level change.
factCheck.reference: IPCC AR6 Working Group I & II Reports on Coastal Systems; EPA Ghana Coastal Zone Management guidelines

whatWeKnow: Human malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites transmitted through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes.

whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Scientists continue researching more effective malaria vaccines, new antimalarial medicines and ways to overcome insecticide resistance.

investigation.title: Paper Model of the Mosquito Life Cycle & Prevention Poster
materials: Published reference diagrams of the mosquito life cycle
steps: Draw the four stages of the mosquito life cycle (egg, larva, pupa, adult) on a poster using textbook diagrams.

investigation.whatToNotice: Interrupting breeding sites and using treated bed nets reduce bites, while clinic testing ensures accurate diagnosis.
investigation.safetyNote: Do NOT collect, keep or breed live mosquitoes or larvae, and do not touch stagnant water.

factCheck.claim: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites and transmitted by infected female Anopheles mosquitoes; fevers require diagnostic testing.
factCheck.explanation: WHO and Ghana Health Service guidelines require parasitological confirmation (by RDT or microscopy) of suspected malaria before treatment.
factCheck.reference: World Health Organization (WHO) World Malaria Report & Ghana Health Service Malaria Case Management Guidelines

learningGoals: Explain why looking at distant stars is looking back in time because light takes time to travel.

Distinguish between established astronomical evidence (thousands of known exoplanets, gravitational observations in galaxies, cosmic expansion) and open questions (the particle nature of dark matter, dark energy, and whether life exists beyond Earth).
Apply media literacy by checking sources and requiring credible evidence before accepting sensational claims.

beforeReading: Ask learners what they have noticed when looking up at the night sky on a clear evening and what questions they have wondered about.
whileReading: Pause at Page 3 for the quick question on why scientists investigate dark matter.
On Page 5 and Page 6, discuss why checking sources matters and why "We do not know yet" is an honest and exciting scientific answer.

discussion: What did Araba mean when she wrote, "Evidence can reveal a mystery without solving every part of it"?
Why is it important to separate an exciting possibility (like life on another planet) from confirmed evidence?

mathsExtension.task: If light from a bright star takes 25 years to reach Earth, how old was the light we see tonight when it left that star?

support: Create a two-column chart on the board titled "What Scientists Have Confirmed" and "Questions Scientists Are Still Investigating".

culturalNotes: Ghana hosts the Ghana Radio Astronomy Observatory at Kuntunse, inspiring young Ghanaian astronomers and engineers.
localiseThis: Encourage learners to observe the night sky from a safe courtyard or veranda with a parent or guardian and sketch the brightest stars or the Moon’s phase.

whatWeKnow: Light travels at a finite speed, so light from distant stars takes years to reach Earth.
Astronomers have confirmed thousands of exoplanets orbiting other stars (including some in binary star systems) and strong evidence for cosmic expansion.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: No confirmed direct detection has yet established the particle nature of dark matter, the nature of dark energy remains an open question, and life beyond Earth has not been confirmed.

investigation.title: Supervised Night-Sky Observation & Evidence vs. Mystery Chart
steps: With a parent or guardian at home in the evening, step into a safe courtyard and observe the night sky for 10 minutes with the naked eye.
Record three things you can directly observe (e.g., Moon phase, differences in star brightness or colour).

investigation.title: Sun or shade?
materials: 6 firm tomatoes of the same size (or another fruit)
steps: Choose one question and say what will change and what will stay the same.
Put 3 on a plate in the sun and 3 on a plate in the shade.
Look, touch gently and draw each day for 5 days.
Repeat with new tomatoes.
Share your results and what you still do not know.
investigation.whatToNotice: Which changes appear first (wrinkling, soft patches, mould)? Are the results the same each time?
investigation.safetyNote: Never eat the tomatoes from the test. Wash hands after handling them and throw spoiled fruit away safely.

teacherGuide.overview: A data-collection story where students do the measuring, find a flaw in their own set-up and report honestly. It respects a farmer’s knowledge while showing why numbers help.
learningGoals: Measure rainfall in millimetres.

Say what a week of data can and cannot show.
beforeReading: Ask learners how they know whether it has rained a lot or a little.

afterReading: Make a class rain gauge and record for at least two weeks.

mathsExtension.task: Add the weekly readings: 0, 12, 0, 0, 5, 0, 0 mm.
What was the average rainfall per day, to one decimal place?

support: Provide a pre-drawn table and a ready-made gauge.
stretch: Compare a gauge in the open with one under a tree for a fortnight and describe the difference.

culturalNotes: Rainfall is vital to farming in Ghana; farmers’ own observations are valuable alongside measurements. Delali, Selorm and Togbe Kwami are verified Ewe names/titles (Togbe means Grandfather in Ewe).

An adult should cut the bottles.

investigation.title: Make a rain gauge
materials: A clear plastic bottle with straight sides (teacher-cut)
steps: An adult cuts the top off the bottle.
Turn the top upside down inside the bottle as a funnel.
Add a little water to level the base and tape the ruler so zero lines up with the water level.
Place the gauge in an open space and read it at the same time each day.
Empty it after reading and record in a table.
investigation.whatToNotice: Do readings differ if the gauge is moved? What changes the numbers?
investigation.safetyNote: An adult must cut the plastic. Do not go outside during thunderstorms.

factCheck.claim: 1 mm of rainfall equals 1 litre of water per square metre.
factCheck.explanation: A depth of 1 mm over 1 square metre is 0.001 cubic metres, which is 1 litre.
factCheck.reference: National meteorological services and the World Meteorological Organization (confirm the exact page before publishing)

reviewerNotes: Confirm open vowel (ɔ) without rhotic r.

teacherGuide.overview: A story that leads learners from curiosity to a small experiment to a balanced conclusion: cell banks are insurance, not a replacement for habitat. Run the tomato test so the idea of ice damage is something they have seen.
learningGoals: Explain what a frozen zoo is and why cells, not animals, are kept.
Explain why freezing can damage living cells and how cryoprotectants help.
Evaluate the claim that technology can replace conservation.

subjectLinks.subject: Our World Our People / Social Studies

beforeReading: Ask: what could happen to a species if its forest is cleared?
whileReading: At page 3, ask learners to predict what the thawed tomato will look like.
afterReading: Run the tomato test and discuss what the slices show.
Debate: “A frozen zoo means we need not worry about extinction.”
discussion: What does a frozen zoo do well, and what can it not do?
Why did Akorfa say a clone is not a species?
reflection: What place near you could be protected, and who could help?

mathsExtension.task: The Frozen Zoo holds about 11,500 cell lines from about 1,300 species and subspecies. About how many cell lines per species on average?
mathsExtension.answer: 11,500 ÷ 1,300 ≈ 8.8, so about 9 cell lines per species or subspecies.

mathsExtension.task: The Frozen Zoo stores cells at about −196 °C and a home freezer at about −18 °C. How much colder is the Frozen Zoo?

support: Provide a labelled diagram of a cell with ice crystals inside.
stretch: Write a short letter to a wildlife officer explaining one thing a cell bank can and cannot do.

culturalNotes: Pangolins live in Ghana’s forests and are shy, ant-eating mammals. The story avoids any claim about how many remain, because numbers change.

localiseThis: Replace pangolins with another local species your learners know.

whatWeKnow: Living cells can be frozen at very low temperatures for long periods and later revived.
Clones of a black-footed ferret and a Przewalski’s horse have been produced from cells banked decades earlier.
Protecting habitat is essential for any wild population.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Whether banked cells can rebuild a healthy, genetically varied wild population for many species.
How best to use cell banks together with habitat protection.

investigation.title: What does freezing do to living cells?
steps: An adult cuts two thin slices.
Keep one slice at room temperature on a plate.
Freeze the other slice overnight.
Thaw it at room temperature next day.
Compare firmness and look with a hand lens, then draw both slices.
investigation.whatToNotice: The thawed slice is softer and leaks water, because ice damaged many of its cells.
investigation.safetyNote: An adult must cut the tomato. Do not eat the test slices. Wash hands afterwards and throw the slices away.

factCheck.claim: The Frozen Zoo in San Diego began in 1975, stores cells at about −196 °C (−320 °F) and holds over 11,500 cell lines from more than 1,300 species and subspecies.

factCheck.reference: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, Frozen Zoo page (check the current numbers).

factCheck.claim: Clones of a black-footed ferret and a Przewalski’s horse were produced from cells banked decades earlier.
factCheck.explanation: Stated on the same page.
factCheck.reference: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, Frozen Zoo page.

factCheck.claim: Ice crystals inside cells can damage them; cryoprotectants and controlled cooling reduce the damage.
factCheck.explanation: Standard cryobiology; not verified from a named page in this session.
factCheck.reference: A cell biology textbook or cryobiology review (to verify).

teacherGuide.overview: A detective story about naming and knowing. Learners practise gathering evidence from a living organism without harming it, then learn why gardens, scientific names and respectful sharing of knowledge matter.
learningGoals: Use observation to identify a plant.

subjectLinks.subject: Our World Our People / Social Studies

beforeReading: Ask learners for different local names for one plant they know.
whileReading: At page 3, ask learners to name three features they could record without touching a tree.
afterReading: Do a leaf-detective walk in the school compound, drawing at least three features of three plants and asking a plant expert or elder for names.
discussion: Why did Maame Ataa say all the names are right?
How could a garden help protect a medicine plant?
reflection: What plant knowledge does your family hold?

mathsExtension.task: The gardens opened in March 1890. How many years ago is that, from 2026?

support: Provide a simple observation chart: leaf shape, roots, fruit, smell.
stretch: Write the two-part scientific name correctly (genus capitalised, species lowercase, both in italics) and explain why.

culturalNotes: Aburi Botanical Gardens, in the Akuapem hills, were officially opened in March 1890 during the colonial period. Today, according to the Botanic Gardens Conservation International listing, its work includes research, conservation of medicinal plants, plant multiplication, horticulture training and environmental education.
Local plant names carry knowledge. Onyina is a Twi name for the silk-cotton tree; confirm local names with speakers before use.
localiseThis: Confirm all local names with speakers of the languages in your class.
Visit a real garden or school plot, with a staff member, if possible; do not pick plants without permission.

investigation.title: Leaf detectives
materials: A plant field guide or help from an adult
steps: Choose three plants in a safe area.
Record leaf shape, size, how leaves are arranged and any other features.
Do not pick or damage plants. Photograph or sketch.
Ask an adult or use a guide to identify them and note local and scientific names.
investigation.whatToNotice: Different plants have different leaves, roots and fruits that act as clues to their identity.
investigation.safetyNote: Do not touch plants you cannot identify, because some can irritate skin. Wash hands afterwards and stay with an adult.

factCheck.claim: Aburi Botanical Gardens were officially opened in March 1890, and today are involved in research, conservation of medicinal plants, plant multiplication, horticulture training and environmental education.
factCheck.explanation: From the Botanic Gardens Conservation International garden listing. The listing is ambiguous about the exact start (land was also cleared in 1899).
factCheck.reference: BGCI, Aburi Botanic Gardens listing.

factCheck.claim: Ceiba pentandra (silk-cotton tree) is known by local names such as onyina in Twi, grows in West Africa and the Americas, and has hand-shaped leaves, buttress roots and kapok fibres.

teacherGuide.overview: A story where children learn why seeds are stored and test the idea that seeds lose their ability to sprout. It links a family story to a national institution and a global backup, and uses real numbers.
learningGoals: Explain that seeds are living and can lose their ability to sprout.
Calculate germination percentages.
Explain why gene banks keep backups.
beforeReading: Ask: do all the foods your grandparents grew still exist today?
whileReading: At page 3, ask learners to predict what will happen to the old seeds.
afterReading: Run a germination test with fresh and old seeds, and compute percentages.
Ask older family members about a food plant that has become rare.
discussion: Why does it matter if a local crop disappears?
Why is a backup in a different country sensible?
reflection: What would you want to save for the future, and why?

mathsExtension.task: 9 of 10 fresh seeds sprouted and 3 of 10 old seeds sprouted. Give the percentages.
The vault’s capacity is 4.5 million samples. Ghana’s 422 samples are what fraction, roughly?
The vault stores at −18 °C. If a room is 28 °C, how many degrees colder is the vault?

support: Provide a table for number planted, number sprouted and percentage.
stretch: Predict what percentage you would expect if you tested a larger sample of 100 seeds, and explain why larger samples are more reliable.

culturalNotes: Ghana’s national gene bank is run by the CSIR-Plant Genetic Resources Research Institute at Bunso, which began in 1964 and has become an institute. Traditional varieties of garden egg, cowpea and other crops are part of Ghanaian food heritage.
The story’s grandmother and variety are invented to show a real challenge: local varieties can disappear from farms.
localiseThis: Use seeds that are common and safe where you teach; do not use treated seeds.
Ask local farmers or elders for the names of traditional varieties.

whatWeKnow: Seeds are living and can stay alive for years when dry and cold, but lose the ability to sprout over time.
Ghana’s gene bank at Bunso holds more than 15,000 accessions, and 422 duplicates were sent to Svalbard in October 2023.
The Svalbard vault keeps seeds at −18 °C, deep in a mountain.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Exactly how long different crops’ seeds stay alive under different storage conditions.
How to store crops that do not make seeds easily, such as some roots and tubers.

investigation.title: Fresh seeds or old seeds?
materials: Two sets of 10 untreated cowpea or bean seeds (one fresh, one old)
steps: Moisten cloth on two trays.
Put the fresh seeds on one and old seeds on the other.
Keep both in the same place, damp but not soaking.
Count how many have sprouted after 3 and 5 days.
Work out the percentages and compare.
investigation.whatToNotice: Fresh seeds usually sprout more than old, poorly stored seeds, but the result with only 10 seeds can vary: try repeating.
investigation.safetyNote: Use untreated seeds only (seeds sold for planting are sometimes coated with chemicals). Do not eat test seeds. Wash hands afterwards.

factCheck.claim: The Ghana National Genebank at Bunso is run by CSIR-PGRRI, began in 1964, and lists more than 15,000 accessions, with yam, cowpea, maize, rice and eggplant among its largest collections.
factCheck.explanation: From the Crop Trust partner page; figures may change.
factCheck.reference: Crop Trust, Ghana National Genebank page.

factCheck.claim: In October 2023 Ghana duplicated 422 accessions (including maize, rice, cowpea and indigenous garden egg) for the Svalbard Global Seed Vault, supported by the Crop Trust; the cost was about US$15,000; Ghana can request the seeds back.
factCheck.explanation: From a Ghana News Agency article dated August 2026.
factCheck.reference: Ghana News Agency, “Ghana deposits 422 germplasm accessions in global seed vault” (August 2026).

factCheck.claim: Svalbard vault: −18 °C, capacity 4.5 million samples, about 120 m into a mountain; depositors own their seeds.
factCheck.explanation: From the Crop Trust FAQ.
factCheck.reference: Crop Trust, Svalbard Global Seed Vault FAQs.

teacherGuide.overview: A story about how scientific ideas change. The oldest known Homo sapiens fossils are in Morocco; Ghana’s cave shows how people lived much later. The timeline walk gives learners a feel for deep time, and the DNA figure supports a conversation about human unity and variation.
learningGoals: Explain that our species is about 300,000 years old and that its origin involved many parts of Africa.
Build and read a scaled timeline.
Explain that people are genetically very similar and that science keeps changing.
beforeReading: Ask: where do you think the story of our species began?
whileReading: At page 5, ask learners to calculate steps before reading on.
afterReading: Build the timeline on the field and add events: school founded, Ghana’s independence (1957), Bosumpra’s first use, Homo sapiens.
Debate: “Why do scientific ideas change?”
discussion: What does it mean that the face looked modern but the braincase did not?
Why is “dispersal within Africa” an important idea?
reflection: What would you like scientists to find next?

mathsExtension.task: On a timeline of 1 step per 10,000 years, how many steps for 300,000 years?
How many years older is Jebel Irhoud (about 300,000) than Herto (about 160,000)?
About 3 billion DNA letters are in a human genome. 0.4% of 3 billion is how many letters?

support: Provide a printed timeline and fill in the dates.
stretch: Explain in one paragraph why a single oldest fossil does not prove where a species began.

culturalNotes: The story presents Ghana as part of the long human story: Bosumpra Cave on the Kwahu Plateau shows human use of a Ghanaian site for more than 10,000 years.
The story treats all people as one species and avoids ranking people or groups.
localiseThis: Add local archaeological sites if available; discuss with care that these are heritage places.
Keep discussion of human variation respectful; be ready to challenge any stereotypes that arise.

whatWeKnow: Fossils from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco, are about 300,000 years old and are the oldest securely dated Homo sapiens fossils.
Early Homo sapiens fossils are known from several parts of Africa, including Florisbad (about 260,000 years), Omo Kibish (about 195,000 years) and Herto (about 160,000 years).
On average, any two people’s genomes are about 99.6% identical.
Bosumpra Cave on the Kwahu Plateau was used for more than 10,000 years.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Exactly where and how our species first emerged, and how groups across Africa interacted.
How early people’s brains, thinking and language developed.
Whether older fossils remain to be found.

investigation.title: Walk through deep time
materials: A long rope or a measured path (at least 30 m)
steps: Choose a scale of 1 step (about 1 m) for 10,000 years.
Mark today as the start of the rope.
Place a marker at 1 step for Bosumpra’s 10,000 years and at 30 steps for Homo sapiens.
Add events your class chooses and discuss what the distances tell you.
investigation.whatToNotice: Human history takes up a very small part of the long history of the Earth.
investigation.safetyNote: Do the walk on a safe, flat area away from roads, in shade where possible.

factCheck.claim: Jebel Irhoud fossils are about 300,000 years old, the oldest securely dated Homo sapiens evidence; the face looks almost modern but the braincase is elongated and archaic; other early sites include Florisbad (about 260,000 years), Omo Kibish (about 195,000 years) and Herto (about 160,000 years).
factCheck.explanation: From the Max Planck Society summary of the 2017 research.
factCheck.reference: Max Planck Society, “The first of our kind” (mpg.de). Check for newer discoveries.

factCheck.claim: On average any two people’s genomes are about 99.6% identical (the older figure of 99.9% counts only single-letter differences).
factCheck.explanation: From the US National Human Genome Research Institute.
factCheck.reference: NHGRI, Human Genomic Variation fact sheet.

factCheck.claim: Bosumpra Cave (Abetifi, Kwahu Plateau) was used over more than 10,000 years; plant remains include Canarium and oil palm, and later domesticated pearl millet and cowpea.
factCheck.explanation: From a published study of the cave’s plant remains.
factCheck.reference: Vegetation History and Archaeobotany, 2015 (Springer); confirm details with an archaeologist.

reviewerNotes: Confirm first-syllable stress and final vowel.

teacherGuide.overview: A story built on a surprising claim. Learners test it by scaling deep time to a rope and then see that birds are living dinosaurs. The rope walk makes huge numbers feel real.
learningGoals: Place events in deep time using a scale.
Explain what happened about 66 million years ago and which dinosaurs survived.
Explain why scientists compare skeletons.
beforeReading: Ask: what is the biggest animal you have ever seen? What do you think lived here long ago?
whileReading: At pages 3 and 4, ask learners to calculate the rope positions before reading.
afterReading: Walk a 150 m scale on the school field with event cards.
Compare a chicken wing or drawing with a theropod diagram.
discussion: Why did the children use a rope?
Why does the hen count as a dinosaur?
reflection: Which fact from the story would you most like to check yourself?

mathsExtension.task: On the rope (1 m = 1 million years), where do humans (300,000 years) fall?
How many years between Jobaria (135 million years ago) and the big extinction (66 million years ago)?
How many times older is the big extinction (66 million years) than our species (300,000 years)?

support: Use a shorter scale, such as 1 cm for every million years on a long paper strip.
stretch: Choose another scale and recalculate the positions. Explain why a good scale makes the numbers easy to compare.

culturalNotes: Village hens are a familiar sight across Ghana and give learners a close link to dinosaurs.
Dinosaur fossils have been found in other African countries, such as Niger and Egypt; the story does not claim any dinosaur has been found in Ghana.
localiseThis: If you cannot lay out 150 m, use a hallway with a scale of 1 cm per million years and mark the main events.
Keep the walk away from roads.

whatWeKnow: Non-bird dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago after an asteroid impact.
Birds are descended from theropod dinosaurs and are living dinosaurs.
Jobaria, a plant-eating dinosaur, lived in what is now Niger about 135 million years ago.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Which dinosaurs lived in different parts of Africa, because large areas have been explored very little.
How different groups of dinosaurs lived and moved.

investigation.title: The deep-time rope
materials: A 150 m rope or measuring tape (or a long paper strip)
steps: Decide the scale: 1 m for 1 million years.
Mark today at the start.
Place markers for Homo sapiens (30 cm), the Lake Bosumtwi crater (about 1.07 m), the big extinction (66 m) and Jobaria (135 m).
Walk the rope and talk about what you notice.
investigation.whatToNotice: People appear in the very first step, and dinosaurs are far away in time.
investigation.safetyNote: Do the walk in a safe area away from traffic and in the shade if possible.

factCheck.claim: Jobaria tiguidensis, a plant-eating sauropod, lived in what is now Niger about 135 million years ago; about 50 specimens were found at one site.
factCheck.explanation: From Penn State’s Earth 105 course page on African geology.
factCheck.reference: Penn State EARTH 105, “Africa Geologic History and Paleontology”.

factCheck.claim: The first Spinosaurus fossils were found in Egypt in 1912 and destroyed in a 1944 bombing raid.
factCheck.explanation: From the same course page. Later discoveries may have added new material.
factCheck.reference: Penn State EARTH 105; check recent literature.

factCheck.claim: About 66 million years ago an asteroid impact led to the extinction of all dinosaurs except birds, and birds descended from theropod dinosaurs.
factCheck.explanation: Standard palaeontology, not verified from a named page in this session.
factCheck.reference: Natural History Museum (London) or Smithsonian resources (to verify).

teacherGuide.overview: A story about weighing explanations against evidence. Learners see how a hypothesis is tested, how clues far away (glass beads, seabed mud) connect to a place at home, and how scientific knowledge sits beside cultural respect.
learningGoals: Compare explanations against evidence.
Explain what a crater and tektites are.
Calculate with large and small numbers, including the area of a circle.

subjectLinks.subject: Mathematics
subjectLinks.link: Area of a circle, large numbers

beforeReading: Ask: why do you think this lake is round?
whileReading: At page 3, ask learners which evidence would support each idea.
afterReading: Make a model crater: drop a marble into a tray of flour covered with cocoa powder (outdoors, with care) and compare crater shapes.
Write a “what we know, think, and are asking” table.
discussion: Why were the children careful to compare ideas rather than choose their favourite?
How do the glass beads connect different places?
reflection: What respectful questions could you ask a community elder about a local landmark?

mathsExtension.task: The lake is about 8.5 km across. What is its radius?
Using π ≈ 3.14, find the area of a circle with a radius of 4.25 km.
How much older is the crater (1.07 million years) than the arrival of Homo sapiens (about 300,000 years)?
The extinction of non-bird dinosaurs was about 66 million years ago. About how many times older is that than the crater?

support: Give a simple table to list each idea and the evidence for and against.
stretch: Research why scientists find impact craters hard to spot on Earth and write a short explanation.

culturalNotes: Lake Bosumtwi is of deep spiritual importance to many Ashanti people, and visitors are often asked to show respect. The story does not describe specific beliefs or rituals; invite local guardians and teachers to share them.
Lake Bosumtwi is listed as a geoheritage site by the International Union of Geological Sciences (IUGS); confirm local details with the Ghana Geological Survey Authority.
localiseThis: Involve the local community, school and traditional authorities in any visit; follow all site rules and customs.
Do not climb into or disturb the lake area.

whatWeKnow: Lake Bosumtwi fills a crater about 10.5 km across that formed about 1.07 million years ago.
The crater is linked to the Ivory Coast tektite field; tiny glass beads have also been found in seabed cores off West Africa.
The impact origin was first suggested in 1931 and later confirmed by shocked rocks and traces of meteorite material.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Details of how life and climate in the region changed over time, which lake mud can reveal.
More about the exact events of the impact.

investigation.title: Make a model crater
steps: Fill the tray with 3 cm of flour and dust the top with cocoa powder.
Drop a marble from 30 cm and measure the crater.
Drop again from 60 cm and compare.
Record the size and shape of each crater.
investigation.whatToNotice: Higher drops make bigger, deeper craters; craters are round even when the object comes in at an angle (unless very low).
investigation.safetyNote: Do this outdoors or on a covered table. Avoid breathing in flour dust and keep children from throwing the marbles.

factCheck.claim: Lake Bosumtwi is in a crater about 1.07 million years old, with a rim diameter of about 10.5 km and a lake diameter of about 8.5 km.
factCheck.explanation: From the IUGS Geoheritage Sites description of the lake.
factCheck.reference: IUGS Geoheritage, “Lake Bosumtwi Impact Crater”.

factCheck.claim: The impact origin was first suggested in 1931; later studies found shocked minerals and meteoritic material; the crater is the source of the Ivory Coast tektite strewn field, with microtektites in deep-sea cores off West Africa.
factCheck.explanation: From the same IUGS description.
factCheck.reference: IUGS Geoheritage, “Lake Bosumtwi Impact Crater”.

factCheck.claim: Many Ashanti people regard Lake Bosumtwi as sacred.
factCheck.explanation: Widely reported; not verified from a named page in this session. The IUGS page mentions local spiritual interest.
factCheck.reference: Ask a local authority or cultural expert to confirm.

reviewerNotes: Confirm local Ashanti Twi pronunciation and spelling preference.

teacherGuide.overview: An adventure that teaches the ocean zones by making the reader descend through them, with a calm problem-solving moment at the snag.
learningGoals: Name the ocean zones and depths.
Explain why colours and light change with depth.
Describe how to respond calmly to a technical problem.
beforeReading: Ask: how deep do you think the ocean goes, and what lives there?
whileReading: At page 4, ask learners to explain the pressure calculation.
afterReading: Make a depth chart on the school wall: 1 cm = 100 m of depth.
Discuss: what decisions would you make as ROV pilot?
discussion: Why did Aba reverse slowly?
How did the team know when to stop?
reflection: What would you like to ask a marine scientist?

mathsExtension.task: The twilight zone is from 200 m to 1,000 m. How thick is it?
Pressure rises by about 1 atmosphere per 10 m. How much extra pressure at 1,000 m?
mathsExtension.answer: 1,000 ÷ 10 = 100 atmospheres more than at the surface.

mathsExtension.task: The deepest point in the Mariana Trench is about 10,994 m. How many times deeper than 1,000 m is that, to the nearest whole number?

support: Provide a depth chart with the zones already coloured.
stretch: Design a deep-sea creature that could live at 1,000 m, and explain how it makes light or finds food.

culturalNotes: Ghana’s coastline faces the Gulf of Guinea. The ship, crew and prize in this story are invented; the zones and measurements are real. Fishing communities hold deep knowledge of the sea; invite a fisher or elder to share.
The story shows a girl taking a technical role and practising calm decision-making.
localiseThis: Invite a local fisher or marine scientist.
Never encourage children to swim or dive into deep water; the story is about a robot.

factCheck.claim: Ocean zones: sunlight zone surface to 200 m; twilight zone 200 m to 1,000 m; midnight zone 1,000 m to 4,000 m with constant darkness except animal bioluminescence; the Mariana Trench’s bottom is about 10,994 m.
factCheck.explanation: From the NOAA JetStream “Layers of the Ocean” page.
factCheck.reference: NOAA, “Layers of the Ocean” (noaa.gov/jetstream/ocean/layers-of-ocean).

factCheck.claim: Pressure rises by about one atmosphere for every 10 metres of depth.
factCheck.explanation: Consistent with NOAA’s figure of more than 5,850 psi at 4,000 m, but not stated in this form on the page.
factCheck.reference: Physics textbook or NOAA Ocean Exploration (to verify).

factCheck.claim: Red light is absorbed quickly in water and blue light travels deepest.
factCheck.explanation: Standard optics; not verified from a named page in this session.
factCheck.reference: NOAA Ocean Exploration or a physics textbook (to verify).

teacherGuide.overview: A science-fiction adventure where the main action is arithmetic and calm teamwork. Learners can recalculate each plan and test what would change if a supply, power level or rescue time changed.
learningGoals: Calculate how long supplies last for several people.
Find the limiting resource and plan ways to extend it.
Discuss leadership, honesty and calm decisions under pressure.
beforeReading: Ask: what do humans need every day to stay alive?
whileReading: At pages 3 to 5, ask learners to do each calculation before the text does.
afterReading: Change one number (for example, the water becomes 48 kg) and recalculate the plan.
Debate: which two roles on the crew mattered most, and why?
discussion: Why was it important to write down every decision?
What was the most important thing the crew did before they started calculating?
reflection: What would you want to be responsible for if you were on the crew?

mathsExtension.task: For 4 people, oxygen use is 1 kg per person per day. How many days does 26 kg last?
Water use is 3 kg per person per day for 4 people. How many days does 60 kg last?
Food use is 0.8 kg per person per day for 4 people. How many days does 24 kg last?
If each person uses 2.5 kg of water a day, and the air dryer returns 4 kg a day, how many days does 60 kg last?
An orbit takes 92 minutes. About how many orbits are there in 24 hours?

support: Provide a table with Supply, Amount, Daily use and Days, ready to fill in.
stretch: Add a fifth crew member to the problem and rebuild the plan. Which resource becomes the limit now?

culturalNotes: This is science fiction: Sankofa Station, the 2064 setting, the cadets and the supply numbers are invented. The astronaut needs, orbit time and number of sunrises are based on real sources.
GhanaSat-1, built by engineers at All Nations University in Ghana, was launched to the International Space Station in June 2017 and released into orbit in July 2017.
“Sankofa” is an Akan idea about learning from the past; the station’s name nods to it.
localiseThis: Label this clearly as fiction. Do not present the numbers as real mission data.
Invite a local science or engineering role model, and connect to Ghana’s own space and satellite work.

whatWeKnow: A person needs oxygen, water and food every day, and the amounts can be estimated.
The International Space Station orbits at about 400 km and takes about 92 minutes to go around Earth.
GhanaSat-1 was built by engineers at All Nations University and launched in 2017.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: How to recycle air and water for very long missions with even greater efficiency.
How best to support people’s mental health on long space missions.

factCheck.claim: Each person needs roughly 0.64 to 1 kg of oxygen, 2.3 to 3.6 kg of drinking water and 0.5 to 0.9 kg of food per day.
factCheck.explanation: From a National Academies table (citing Eckart, 1996). The story rounds up to simple numbers.
factCheck.reference: National Academies, “Advanced Technology for Human Support in Space” (1997), Table 2-1.

factCheck.claim: The ISS orbits at about 400 km, takes about 92 minutes per orbit and crews see 16 sunrises and sunsets a day.
factCheck.explanation: From the European Space Agency.
factCheck.reference: ESA, “Where is the International Space Station?”

factCheck.claim: GhanaSat-1 was built by All Nations University engineers, launched 3 June 2017 to the ISS, and released on 7 July 2017; it is a 1U CubeSat about 10 cm on each side and about 1 kg.
factCheck.explanation: From a Wikipedia summary of the project.
factCheck.reference: Wikipedia, “GhanaSat-1” (confirm with All Nations University).

teacherGuide.overview: A gentle bedtime spooky story that teaches a calming habit: look closely, then look again. A touch of magic (the glowing thread) sits beside a real explanation (a coat on a wardrobe).
learningGoals: Name a common night-time fear and a way to face it.
Use “look again” to test a worry.
Retell the story in order.
beforeReading: Ask: what is a shadow, and how is it made?
whileReading: At page 6, ask: what did Nutifafa see when he looked closely?
afterReading: Make shadow shapes with a torch and objects, then guess each shadow.
Draw the “monster” and then draw what it really was.
discussion: Why did Nutifafa look twice?
Who can you tell when you are scared?
reflection: What can you do the next time something looks scary?

mathsExtension.task: A spider has 8 legs. How many legs do 3 spiders have?

support: Use picture cards to put the story in order.

teacherGuide.overview: A foggy-lake adventure in which a possibly magical light tests a child’s judgement. The lessons are practical: life jackets, staying calm, listening, and not following what you do not understand.
learningGoals: Explain how fog forms in simple terms.
Describe how sound can guide people in fog.
Discuss why children must not follow strange lights.
beforeReading: Ask: how can you find your way when you cannot see?
whileReading: At page 4, ask learners to explain Kofiga’s two rules.
afterReading: Make fog in a jar with warm water, ice and a match-free method your teacher approves.
Write a safety poster for people who travel on the water.
discussion: Why did Kofiga refuse to follow the light?
How did sound help them?
reflection: What safety rules do you follow near water?

mathsExtension.task: The crossing normally takes 20 minutes. The fog made it take 3 times as long. How long did it take?
Enam blew her whistle 4 times each minute for 15 minutes. How many blasts?

support: Provide a sound-and-direction diagram.
stretch: Design a safety kit for a small boat and explain each item.

culturalNotes: Lake Volta is one of the world’s largest man-made lakes by surface area, created after the Akosombo Dam. The family, canoe and crossing are invented. Many fishing communities live and work on its shores.
Old stories of lights on the water are treated with respect; the story offers several possible explanations and does not insist on one.
localiseThis: Involve a local fisher, a swimming or water-safety instructor and the local boat-safety rules.
Always teach life jackets, adult supervision and never travelling in fog without adults.

factCheck.claim: Fog can form when cool air sits over warmer water or when air cools to its dew point near the surface.
factCheck.explanation: General meteorology; the story states a simplified version.
factCheck.reference: Ghana Meteorological Agency or a weather textbook (to verify).

factCheck.claim: Lake Volta was created by the Akosombo Dam and is one of the largest man-made lakes by surface area.
factCheck.explanation: Widely stated; confirm the latest ranking.
factCheck.reference: Volta River Authority (to verify).

reviewerNotes: Confirm nasalized final vowel in Ewe (gã).

culturalNotes: The harmattan is a dry, dusty wind that crosses West Africa in the dry season, typically from about late November to March. The school, characters and events are invented.

reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?

teacherGuide.overview: A “partly solved” mystery. It shows that science can answer one part of a story (what the tested samples were) while leaving other parts open.
learningGoals: Explain what evidence and DNA are in simple terms.
Separate what is solved from what is still unknown.
Show respect for stories and ask for proof.
beforeReading: Locate the Himalayas on a map. Ask: what stories do you know about forest creatures?
whileReading: At page 5, ask: does this solve everything?
afterReading: Make two lists, Solved and Not solved, for another legend.
Compare a yeti story with a Ghanaian forest story.
discussion: Why is it important to test samples?
Why do people keep telling the story?
reflection: What is a mystery you would like to solve?

mathsExtension.task: In the study, 9 samples were labelled “yeti”. If 8 were bears and 1 was a dog, what fraction were bears?

support: Provide a Solved / Not solved table with pictures.
stretch: Write a short report: “What the DNA can and cannot tell us.”

culturalNotes: The Himalayas are on the other side of the world from Ghana. The pupils, school and teacher are invented. People in the Himalayas hold the yeti stories as part of their own culture, and the story treats them with respect.
Ghana has its own stories of forest creatures. Pupils may share them to compare how communities explain the unknown.
localiseThis: Invite elders to share local forest stories and discuss how people explain things they cannot see.
Keep the tone respectful of every culture’s stories.

whatWeKnow: Nearly all the samples tested in the 2017 study came from bears, with one from a dog.
Bears can stand on two legs and leave large footprints.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: What every person who reported a yeti actually saw.
Whether any unknown large animal lives in the high mountains (there is no evidence so far).

factCheck.claim: A 2017 study by Charlotte Lindqvist’s team tested samples said to be yeti; they came from Himalayan and Tibetan brown bears and an Asian black bear, with one dog sample; the study linked legends to real bears.
factCheck.explanation: From National Geographic’s report. Sample counts differ in the article: nine “yeti” samples, 24 in all.
factCheck.reference: National Geographic, “Yeti legends: real animals, DNA, bears, Himalaya, science” (2017); original paper in Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

teacherGuide.overview: An “open, and probably empty” mystery that teaches evidence-checking: a real hole and a famous story, but no proof of treasure. It also sends a strong safety message.
learningGoals: Explain the difference between evidence and legend.
Say why blurry images are not proof.
Describe the dangers of digging deep holes.
beforeReading: Ask: have you heard a story about buried treasure? How could we check it?
whileReading: At page 5, ask: what would count as real proof?
afterReading: Make a Known / Not known chart for another local legend.
Discuss safe ways to explore history, such as museums and archaeology.
discussion: Why did people keep digging?
What evidence would change your mind?
reflection: What can we learn from a mystery with no answer?

mathsExtension.task: 1795 to 2026: how many years since the pit was found?

support: Provide a timeline with the key dates.
stretch: Compare evidence for Oak Island treasure with the evidence for a real archaeological find.

culturalNotes: Oak Island is in Mahone Bay off Nova Scotia, Canada. Pupils may compare it with Ghanaian stories of hidden gold and the gold-weights and royal treasures of the Asante, which are real cultural heritage, not buried-pit legends.
The story presents the pit as a legend without proof and encourages critical thinking about “get rich quick” treasure stories.
localiseThis: Link to Ghana’s real treasures: Asante gold-weights, regalia and museum collections.
Never encourage digging deep holes; stress that real investigations are done by trained teams with permission.

whatWeKnow: The pit is real and has been dug since 1795; salt water floods it; no treasure has been found.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Who made the pit, why, and whether any treasure was ever there.

factCheck.claim: Oak Island is in Mahone Bay, Nova Scotia; Daniel McGinnis found the depression in 1795; diggers reached about 9 m, then about 30 m in 1804 when salt water flooded the shaft; no treasure has been found; four treasure hunters died in a 1965 accident; a 1971 camera produced faint images.
factCheck.explanation: From The Canadian Encyclopedia.
factCheck.reference: The Canadian Encyclopedia, “Oak Island.”

reflection: What would you build with your community?

teacherGuide.overview: A heritage mystery about an unwritten past. It shows how oral history is a real kind of record and how historians check stories using several kinds of evidence, with respect for the community that keeps them.
learningGoals: Explain oral history and why it matters.

whileReading: At page 5, ask learners to name two ways to check an oral story.
afterReading: Interview an elder about a story of your community (with permission).

discussion: Why is oral history valuable?
How should visitors behave in a community?
reflection: Which story of your family would you want to keep?

whatWeKnow: Nzulezo is a real stilt village on Lake Tadane in Ghana’s Western Region.

whatWeAreStillDiscovering: How historians and archaeologists can add other evidence to the community’s own account.

factCheck.reference: Ghana Museums and Monuments Board, “Nzulezu Stilt Settlement” (gmmb.gov.gh).

teacherGuide.overview: A heritage mystery where two kinds of evidence, oral history and archaeology, give partly different answers. Learners practise weighing them rather than choosing a side.
learningGoals: Explain how archaeologists find clues about a vanished town.
Compare oral history with archaeological evidence.
Describe why heritage sites should not be dug up or looted.

subjectLinks.subject: Social Studies / History
subjectLinks.link: Trade and towns in pre-colonial Ghana

beforeReading: Ask: how can we learn about a town nobody lives in any more?
whileReading: At page 6, ask learners to draw the two timelines.
afterReading: Draw two timelines for the end of Begho (oral history and archaeology) and mark where they differ.
Interview an elder about the history of your own town, with permission.
discussion: What does each kind of evidence do best?
Why should heritage sites be protected?
Teacher note: some sources list people among the goods traded through Begho. For older learners, you may discuss this carefully, linking to your syllabus and to local memory.
reflection: What would you like a future archaeologist to know about your town?

mathsExtension.task: If between 7,000 and 10,000 people lived in Begho, what is the difference between the highest and lowest estimates?
Oral history places the destruction around 1750; some evidence suggests people stayed into the early 1800s (say 1810). About how many years apart are those two accounts?
mathsExtension.answer: About 60 years. The gap shows why the accounts conflict and why more evidence is needed.

support: Provide a two-column chart: Oral history / Archaeology.
stretch: Write a short paragraph arguing which evidence best explains the end of Begho, and what new evidence would help.

culturalNotes: Begho is a real archaeological site in the Bono region, near Hani. The children, Nana Afriyie and Dr Mensima are invented. Descendants of its people live in several communities, and their accounts deserve respect.
The story presents oral tradition as real evidence that historians weigh alongside archaeology, and it does not decide between them.
localiseThis: Use your local heritage sites and invite a museum or heritage officer.

whatWeKnow: Begho was a large trading town near Hani, with thousands of people.
It was excavated by archaeologists in the twentieth century.
People today trace their families to refugees from Begho.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Exactly when the town began and when and how it ended, since the accounts do not agree.
The full layout of the town, since only parts have been excavated.

factCheck.claim: Begho (near Hani, Bono) was a large trading town; sources give its start as around the 11th century or earlier; its pottery scatter was large; at least five quarters and 1,000 to 1,500 house mounds were found; peak population is estimated at 7,000 to 10,000; oral tradition says the Asante destroyed it, placed around the mid-18th century, while some archaeological evidence suggests a reduced town into the early 19th century.
factCheck.explanation: From Wikipedia’s “Begho” article, which cites scholarly works; the page does not resolve the conflict between accounts. The story gives dates as conflicting claims, not facts.
factCheck.reference: Wikipedia, “Begho” (reference list includes Merrick Posnansky, “Begho: Life and Times,” Journal of West African History 1(2): 95–118, 2015, and Ivor Wilks, “The Northern Factor in Ashanti History: Begho and the Mande,” Journal of African History 2(1): 25–34, 1961; these were not opened in this session and should be checked directly).

teacherGuide.overview: A mystery about meaning: archaeologists can tell what people ate and used, but not why they shaped small clay animals. The story separates known, debated and unknown.
learningGoals: Explain what charred seeds, bones and pottery can show.
Distinguish what is known from what is only guessed.
Explain why ancient sites and objects must be protected.
beforeReading: Ask: if someone found your pencil case in 3,000 years, what could they guess about you?
whileReading: At page 5, invite guesses for why the clay animals were made.
afterReading: Make a small clay animal and write a museum label saying what is known and not known.
Plan a class “museum” with clear rules for handling objects.
discussion: Why can we know what people ate but not why they made a toy or figure?
Why should we leave ancient objects where they are?
reflection: What would you want to leave for people in the future?

mathsExtension.task: One source says 2500 to 1400 BCE. How long is that span?
Watson says the tradition appeared about 3,600 to 3,200 years ago. How long is that span?
mathsExtension.answer: 400 years. The two sources describe spans of very different lengths, which is part of the puzzle.

mathsExtension.task: About what year BCE was 3,600 years ago? (Use 2026 and ignore the missing year 0.)

support: Provide a Known / Debated / Unknown chart with pictures.
stretch: Compare the Kintampo evidence with the evidence from Begho and decide which gives a fuller picture.

culturalNotes: The Kintampo complex is a real archaeological tradition in Ghana. The pupils and guide are invented. The clay animals found at Boyase Hill and Ntereso are real kinds of finds.
The story is clear that nobody knows why the animals were made, and does not give them a religious meaning.
localiseThis: Visit a local museum or invite a curator.
Never collect or dig up ancient objects; report finds to local heritage authorities.

whatWeKnow: People of the Kintampo complex lived in Ghana more than 3,000 years ago, farming, herding and hunting.
They made pottery, polished stone tools and small clay animals.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: When exactly the tradition began and ended, since sources give different ranges.
Where the people came from.
Why they made the clay animals and what the animals meant.

factCheck.claim: The Kintampo tradition is found near Nkoranza and Techiman; evidence includes pearl millet, oil palm, yams, cowpea, goats, sheep, cattle and dogs; clay animal figures at Boyase Hill and Ntereso have unknown meaning; origins are debated; dates are given as about 2500 to 1400 BCE in one source and about 3,600 to 3,200 years ago (BP) by Watson.
factCheck.explanation: Watson’s review (a scholarly article, verified by its abstract on the University of Ghana repository) gives c. 3600 to 3200 BP. The 2500 to 1400 BCE range comes from Wikipedia’s “Kintampo Complex” article, a summary. The story shows both and lets readers question the difference.
factCheck.reference: D. J. Watson, “Within savanna and forest: A review of the Late Stone Age Kintampo Tradition, Ghana,” Azania: Archaeological Research in Africa 45(2): 141–174 (2010), doi:10.1080/0067270X.2010.491361; and Wikipedia, “Kintampo Complex”.

learningGoals: Explain the lost-wax method in simple steps.
Describe how a balance and weights work.
Discuss why some meanings are lost and how we might recover them.
beforeReading: Ask: how would you weigh something small without a modern scale?
whileReading: At page 4, ask learners to do the mithqal sum.
afterReading: Make wax or clay models of proverb figures and write the proverb on a label.
Invite an elder to explain a proverb or adinkra symbol.
discussion: Why might a proverb be shaped as an object?
What could help us decode a pattern?
reflection: What proverb would you shape into an object?

mathsExtension.task: One mithqal is about 4.6 g. How many grams are 3 mithqal?
A weight of 23 g is how many mithqal?
If a trader adds 0.4 g of lead to a 4.2 g weight, what is the new weight?

support: Provide pictures of the weights and a simple balance to try.
stretch: Choose an adinkra symbol or proverb and explain how you could turn it into a weight design.

culturalNotes: Akan goldweights are real objects found in museums around the world. The children, Mrs Konadu and the museum are invented. Adinkra symbols and proverbs are living Akan traditions; pupils should learn them from the communities who keep them.
The story presents museum scholarship and says plainly that much remains unknown, including whether the figurative pieces were mainly weights or reminders of proverbs.
localiseThis: Use local proverbs and invite elders to explain them.
Do not copy sacred shrine designs; learn about them from the communities who hold them.

whatWeKnow: The weights were cast in brass by the lost-wax method and used in trade, with gold dust as a major currency.
Geometric weights are older and figurative weights came later.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: What most geometric patterns mean.
How many figurative pieces were weights and how many were reminders of proverbs.

factCheck.claim: Almost all Akan goldweights are brass, cast by the lost-wax method; geometric weights date to the 1400s and figurative weights appear around 1600; recent scholarship suggests geometric weights mainly weighed gold dust and that many figurative pieces may have embodied proverbs; some followed the Arab mithqal (about 4.6 g); the meaning of most geometric designs is unknown.
factCheck.explanation: From The Metropolitan Museum of Art’s collection page on a stool gold weight.
factCheck.reference: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, “Stool gold weight” (metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/317686).

teacherGuide.overview: A ballad with a strong national theme, a good model of the form and devices that BECE poetry questions test. Form: six quatrains (four-line stanzas) with rhyme scheme ABCB (the second and fourth lines rhyme). Devices: simile (like morning mist), metaphor (freedom is a road, a nation is a shield), personification (the morning rose; the drums spoke), symbolism (red, gold, green, Black Star, lantern), imagery, alliteration (safe and sound), repetition (green/gold/red anaphora). Tone: proud and hopeful. Theme: freedom is a responsibility that each generation must carry on.

teacherGuide.overview: A free-verse poem that demonstrates the devices BECE questions test. Form: free verse in six stanzas (a tercet followed by five quatrains; no end-rhyme). Devices: simile (like a bird, like a hen), metaphor (each sum is a seed; the road is a black river; the moon is a cracked coin), personification (the classroom swallows the dark; fear stands with arms folded), imagery (sight and sound), symbolism (lantern as hope and learning), contrast (dark and light), and a shift of voice in the last stanza. Tone: quiet, then hopeful. Theme: determination and education as a beacon.
learningGoals: Identify free verse and explain how it differs from rhymed verse.
Identify simile, metaphor and personification with quotations.
Explain the symbol of the lantern and the theme.

beforeReading: Ask: what does the word beacon bring to mind?
whileReading: At each stanza, ask learners to find one device and say what it adds.
afterReading: Write a short paragraph: “How does the poet present determination?” using three quotations.

discussion: Why does the poet use animals and seeds to describe studying?
What is the effect of the last stanza changing to “I”?
reflection: What is the “lantern” in your life?

support: Provide a device table with the quotations already filled in.
stretch: Compare how this poem and a rhymed poem present hope.

culturalNotes: Power cuts and studying by lantern or phone light are familiar to many Ghanaian students. The poem is original and is about determination, not about blaming anyone.
The title word beacon links to the “Beacon of Light” idea of education as a guiding light, as in the BECE literature anthology.
localiseThis: Link to learners’ own experiences with studying in hard conditions, without blaming anyone.
Do not encourage study by candle or open flame near anything flammable; use safe lights.

teacherGuide.overview: A Shakespearean (English) sonnet on a Ghanaian subject. Form: 14 lines in three quatrains and a closing couplet, rhyme scheme ABAB CDCD EFEF GG, roughly ten syllables a line. Devices: imagery (colour and process), contrast (the farmer’s hard work and the distant chocolate bar), irony (someone smiles, unknowing whose the toil), metaphor (pride is rooted deeper than the soil), alliteration (days, daily, dreams), and a turn in the third quatrain. Tone: respectful and gently critical. Theme: appreciation of the people behind our food.
learningGoals: Recognise a Shakespearean sonnet and its rhyme scheme.
Identify imagery, irony and metaphor with quotations.
Explain the theme and the effect of the closing couplet.

teacherGuide.overview: A story that shows how a people remembers its past through tradition and how historians test it. It teaches the difference between a story told by a community, evidence from archaeology, and a date that is still uncertain.
learningGoals: Retell the Ewe tradition of Notsé.
Explain what archaeologists and historians add to a tradition.
Explain why a date may be uncertain.
beforeReading: Ask: who tells the history of your family? Is it written or spoken?
whileReading: At page 4, ask learners to name one detail that is tradition and one that is evidence.
afterReading: Interview an elder about a family story and note which details are certain and which are told differently by different people.
Draw the groups leaving Notsé on a map.
discussion: Why might two accounts of the same event differ?
Why is it useful to keep both the tradition and the evidence?
reflection: What story do you carry that tells people where you come from?

mathsExtension.task: If Agokoli’s reign is given as 1670 to 1720, how many years is that?
From the fifteenth century (1400s) to now is at least how many years? Use 1400 and 2026.

support: Provide a two-column chart: Tradition / Evidence.
stretch: Research another people’s story of migration in Ghana and compare how it is told.

culturalNotes: Hogbetsotso is celebrated by the Anlo Ewe, usually on the first Sunday in November. The story is told in a family voice. The family and children are invented.
The story separates oral tradition from what historians and archaeologists have found, and shows both with respect.
Spellings (Agokoli or Agorkoli, Notsé or Notsie) vary between sources.
localiseThis: Invite an Ewe elder or cultural officer to tell the tradition in their own words.
Use local place names for the dispersal map.

whatWeKnow: A large movement of people from Notsé is widely accepted.
Archaeologists have found the remains of an enclosure at Notsé and read it as sacred and symbolic.
The Anlo celebrate Hogbetsotso, the festival of the exodus.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: The exact date of the exodus.
Whether the wall was broken through, since the enclosure may not have been finished.
Whether Notsé was the true beginning of the Ewe or one great journey in a longer history.

factCheck.claim: The exodus of the Ewe from Notsé is generally placed in the 16th to 17th centuries; Agokoli’s reign is given as 1670 to 1720; archaeologists read the enclosure as sacred and symbolic; some historians doubt the breach story because the enclosure may be unfinished; the dispersal produced groups that settled around Hohoe, Kpando, Peki, Ho and the coast.
factCheck.explanation: From Wikipedia’s article on the exodus, which also notes that historians question whether Notsé was the true origin of the Ewe and that colonial scholars and missionaries shaped how the story spread.
factCheck.reference: Wikipedia, “Exodus of the Ewe from Notsé”. Check also scholarly work and Ewe cultural authorities.

factCheck.claim: Hogbetsotso is celebrated by the Anlo on the first Sunday of November; tradition says women poured water to weaken the wall and the people walked backwards to mislead pursuers.
factCheck.explanation: From a Ghana travel article that describes these details as custom and tradition, not documented history.
factCheck.reference: Ghana Travel (ghanatrvl.com), “Hogbetsotso Festival”.

factCheck.claim: Another account places the Notsé period in the 15th or 16th century and names different Ewe groups and journeys.
factCheck.explanation: From a community site on Ghanaian place names, which notes that these accounts rest largely on oral tradition and secondary sources.
factCheck.reference: Ghana place names (sites.google.com/site/ghanaplacenames), “Ewe”.

learningGoals: Explain what Homowo means and why it is celebrated.
Describe how the festival food is prepared and shared.
Explain why the date can change from year to year.
beforeReading: Ask: what festival does your family celebrate? What does it remember?
whileReading: At page 3, ask learners what the story says and what the tellers disagree about.
afterReading: Draw the stages of the Homowo season in order.
Interview an adult about a festival in your community.
discussion: Why is it important to share food during a festival?
Why might a date not be fixed?
reflection: What would you hoot at, to show you are no longer afraid of it?

mathsExtension.task: The noise ban lasts four weeks and two days. How many days is that?

support: Provide pictures of the stages and ask learners to put them in order.
stretch: Compare Homowo with a harvest festival from another part of Ghana.

culturalNotes: Homowo is the festival of the Ga people of Greater Accra. The family is invented. The details of rites and food come from published accounts and vary between Ga towns and families.
The origin of the festival is told as tradition, and accounts differ on whether the famine happened during the migration or in early settlement.
The date follows the Ga calendar and is announced by the priests and elders; it is usually in August, sometimes July or September.
localiseThis: Use the local Ga announcements and customs; invite a Ga elder or cultural officer.
Follow local rules about food, libation and photographs.

whatWeKnow: Homowo is a Ga festival linked to hunger, harvest and thanksgiving.
The date follows the Ga calendar and changes slightly each year.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Where and when the famine in the origin story took place.
Which grain the dish was first made from, since accounts mention millet and corn.

factCheck.claim: Homowo is traced to famine during the Ga migration; the name combines homo (hunger) and wo (hoot); kpokpoi is made from steamed dough mixed with palm oil and okra; each family sprinkles some on the ground for the ancestors; there is a noise ban of four weeks and two days; the Twins Yam Festival is the Friday before; the festival is usually in August, occasionally in July or September.
factCheck.explanation: From Wikipedia’s Homowo article, which itself notes that dates vary, that origin accounts differ and that several sources are informal.
factCheck.reference: Wikipedia, “Homowo”. Check also Ga cultural authorities and scholarly sources.

teacherGuide.overview: A story about unity and about how historians work. It teaches how small states joined against a larger power, why symbols matter and why two sources can give different dates.
learningGoals: Explain why the states joined together and how.
Describe the union’s symbols and rules.
Compare two dates for the same event and explain why they might differ.

beforeReading: Do the stick demonstration with learners before reading.
whileReading: At page 5, ask learners to write both dates and give two reasons they might differ.
afterReading: Make a bundle of sticks or straws and explain the lesson to a partner.
Write a short speech urging cooperation, in the voice of a leader at the union’s founding.
discussion: Why was a shared symbol important?

reflection: How can your class become like a bundle?

mathsExtension.task: If Feyiase was in 1700, how many years ago was it from 2026? And if 1701?

culturalNotes: The Asante union is a major part of Ghana’s history. This story uses published accounts and an invented teacher and pupils. The Golden Stool is sacred; the story refers to it briefly and with respect.
The saying about one stick and a bundle is told in many parts of Africa and is used here as a classroom teaching device, not as a quotation from a particular source.
The meaning of the name Asante is told as an explanation people give, not as settled fact.
localiseThis: Invite a local historian or a member of the community to speak.
Follow local custom when speaking about chiefs and the Golden Stool.

whatWeKnow: Denkyira dominated its neighbours in the late 1600s and was defeated by the Asante union at Feyiase.
The Golden Stool became a symbol of unity.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: The exact year of Feyiase, which one source gives as August 1701 and another as 1700.
The details of how Denkyira’s king died, which accounts describe differently.

factCheck.claim: Osei Tutu and Okomfo Anokye founded the Asante kingdom around the end of the 17th century; Denkyira conquered neighbouring kingdoms in the last decade of the century; the union’s victory at Feyiase in 1700 ended Denkyira rule; the Golden Stool is the seal of the union; Odwira and a politico-military constitution were set up; between 1700 and 1750 the union grew to cover an area larger than modern Ghana.
factCheck.explanation: From the Manhyia Palace Archives’ account of the Asante union, which says Anokye “is believed” to have called the stool and gives many dates as approximate.
factCheck.reference: Manhyia Palace Museum / Archives, “History of Asante Union”.

factCheck.claim: The Battle of Feyiase took place in August 1701 between the Asante (under Osei Tutu) and Denkyira (under Ntim Gyakari); Denkyira had a few Dutch cannons; Ntim Gyakari was killed; the Asante captured the cannons.
factCheck.explanation: From Wikipedia’s article on the battle, which cites academic sources and notes uncertainty about the cannon count and the account of the king’s death.
factCheck.reference: Wikipedia, “Battle of Feyiase”.

culturalNotes: This story is about the origins of Dagbon as told by the drummers and in published accounts. The elder and children are invented. Many parts are oral tradition, and tellers differ on names, order and dates.

Dagbon’s traditions belong to its people. Permission should be sought from Dagbon traditional authorities before this story is published.

whatWeKnow: Dagbon’s history is kept by drummers and elders and has been written down by researchers.

whatWeAreStillDiscovering: The dates of the kingdom’s beginnings, which sources place in the 13th or 14th century.
